Syllabus
Course Structure Class X

UNIT I: NUMBER SYSTEMS
1.	 REAL NUMBERS	 (15 Periods)

Euclid’s division lemma, Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic - statements after 
reviewing work done earlier and after illustrating and motivating through examples,
Proofs of irrationality of 2 , 3 , 5 ,  Decimal representation of rational numbers in
terms of terminating/non-terminating recurring decimals.

UNIT II: ALGEBRA
1.	 POLYNOMIALS	 (7 Periods)

Zeroes of a polynomial. Relationship between zeroes and coefficients of quadratic
polynomials. Statement and simple problems on division algorithm for polynomials
with real coefficients.

2.	 PAIR OF LINEAR EQUATIONS IN TWO VARIABLES	 (15 Periods)
	 Pair of linear equations in two variables and graphical method of their solution, consistency/

inconsistency. 
	 Algebraic conditions for number of solutions. Solution of a pair of linear equations in two 

variables algebraically - by substitution, by elimination and by cross-multiplication method. 
Simple situational problems. Simple problems on equations reducible to linear equations.

3.	 Quadratic Equations	 (15 Periods)
	 Standard form of a quadratic equation ax2 + bx + c = 0, (a ≠ 0). Solutions of quadratic equations 

(only real roots) by factorisation, and by using quadratic formula. Relationship between 
discriminant and nature of roots.

	 Situational problems based on quadratic equations related to day to day activities to be 
incorporated.

4.	 Arithemetic Progressions	 (8 Periods)
	 Motivation for studying Arithmetic Progression, Derivation of the nth term and sum of the first 

n terms of A.P. and their application in solving daily life problems.

UNIT III: Coordinate Geometry
1.	 Lines (In two-dimensions)	 (14 Periods)
	 Review: Concepts of coordinate geometry, graphs of linear equations. Distance formula. 

Section formula (internal division). Area of a triangle.



UNIT IV: Geometry
1.	 Triangles	 (15 Periods)
	 Definitions, examples, counter examples of similar triangles.
	 1.	 (Prove) If a line is drawn parallel to one side of a triangle to intersect the other two 

sides in distinct points, the other two sides are divided in the same ratio.
	 2.	 (Motivate) If a line divides two sides of a triangle in the same ratio, the line is parallel 

to the third side.
	 3.	 (Motivate) If in two triangles, the corresponding angles are equal, their corresponding 

sides are proportional and the triangles are similar.
	 4.	 (Motivate) If the corresponding sides of two triangles are proportional, their 

corresponding angles are equal and the two triangles are similar.
	 5.	 (Motivate) If one angle of a triangle is equal to one angle of another triangle and the 

sides including these angles are proportional, the two triangles are similar.
	 6.	 (Motivate) If a perpendicular is drawn from the vertex of the right angle of a right 

triangle to the hypotenuse, the triangles on each side of the perpendicular are similar 
to the whole triangle and to each other.

	 7.	 (Prove) The ratio of the areas of two similar triangles is equal to the ratio of the squares 
of their corresponding sides.

	 8.	 (Prove) In a right triangle, the square on the hypotenuse is equal to the sum of the 
squares on the other two sides.

	 9.	 (Prove) In a triangle, if the square on one side is equal to sum of the squares on the 
other two sides, the angles opposite to the first side is a right angle.

2.	 Circles	 (8 Periods)
	 Tangent to a circle at, point of contact
	 1.	 (Prove) The tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through 

the point of contact.
	 2.	 (Prove) The lengths of tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal.

3.	 CONSTRUCTIONS	 (8 Periods)
	 1. 	Division of a line segment in a given ratio (internally).
	 2.	 Tangents to a circle from a point outside it.
	 3.	 Construction of a triangle similar to a given triangle.

UNIT V: TRIGONOMETRY

1.	 INTRODUCTION TO TRIGONOMETRY 	 (10 Periods)
	 Trigonometric ratios of an acute angle of a right-angled triangle. Proof of their existence 

(well defined); motivate the ratios whichever are defined at 0° and 90°. Values (with 
proofs) of the trigonometric ratios of 30°, 45° and 60°. Relationships between the ratios.

2.	 TRIGONOMETRIC IDENTITIES	 (15 Periods)
	 Proof and applications of the identity sin2A + cos2A = 1. Only simple identities to be 

given. Trigonometric ratios of complementary angles.



3.	 Heights and distances: Angle of Elevation, Angle of Depression.	(8 Periods)
	 Simple problems on heights and distances. Problems should not involve more than two 

right triangles. Angles of elevation / depression should be only 30°, 45°, 60°.

UNIT VI: MENSURATION

1.	 AREAS RELATED TO CIRCLES	 (12 Periods)
	 Motivate the area of a circle; area of sectors and segments of a circle. Problems based 

on areas and perimeter / circumference of the above said plane figures. (In calculating 
area of segment of a circle, problems should be restricted to central angle of 60°, 90° and 
120° only. Plane figures involving triangles, simple quadrilaterals and circle should be 
taken.)

2.	 SURFACE AREAS AND VOLUMES	 (12 Periods)
	 1. 	Surface areas and volumes of combinations of any two of the following: cubes, cuboids, 

spheres, hemispheres and right circular cylinders/cones. Frustum of a cone.
	 2.	 Problems involving converting one type of metallic solid into another and other 

mixed problems. (Problems with combination of not more than two different solids 
be taken).

UNIT VII: STATISTICS AND PROBABILITY

1.	 STATISTICS	 (18 Periods)
	 Mean, median and mode of grouped data (bimodal situation to be avoided). Cumulative 

frequency graph.

2.	 PROBABILITY	 (10 Periods)
	 Classical definition of probability. Simple problems on finding the probability of an 

event.

CONCEPT – 1 : EUCLID’S DIVISION LEMMA
To find HCF of two numbers we teachers teach our students (class VII) a method 

known as long division method. This long division algorithm is absolutely based on Euclid’s 
division lemma. 

Difference Between Algorithm and Lemma 
(a)	 Algorithm : An algorithm is a series of well defined steps which gives a procedure 

for solving a type of problem. 
(b)	 Lemma : It is proven statement used for proving another statement. 

State Euclid’s Division Lemma
Statement 

If a and b be two given positive integers, such that a > b then there exist unique integers 
q and r such that a = b × q + r, 0 ≤ r < b. It is known as Euclid’s division lemma. 

Note: Euclid’s division algorithm (long division method) is based on Euclid’s division Lemma.

Euclid’s Division Algorithm
Euclid’s division algorithm is a technique to compute the Highest Common factor 
(HCF) of two given positive integers. 
Steps required in finding the HCF of two distinct positive integers by using the method 
of division algorithm are as follow: 
	 1.	 Let two given distinct positive integers are a and b. Take the larger positive integer 

as ‘a’ and the smaller positive integer as ‘b’. 
	 2.	 Divide ‘a’ by ‘b’ and represent quotient so obtained by ‘q’ and remainder by r. 
	 3.	 If r = 0 then declare that ‘b’ is HCF of a and b. 

1

S chand Mathematics for Class X



2    S. Chand’s MATHEMATICS FOR CLASS X

	 4.	 If remainder (r) obtained in step number 2 is not zero then take ‘b’ as dividend 
and ‘r’ as divisor. 

	 5.	 Now after division of ‘b’ by ‘r’ represent quotient so obtained by ‘q1’ and remainder 
so obtained by  r1.

	 6.	 Now check that if r1 = 0, then q1 will be HCF of a and b. 
	 7.	 If r1 ≠ 0 then take r1 as divisor and ‘q1’ as dividend to obtain new quotient (q2) and 

new remainder (r2).
	 8.	 This process will remain continue till the remainder comes out zero. 
	 9.	 In which steps of division the remainder comes zero the divisor of that step (i.e. 

last divisor) is known as HCF of two given distinct positive integers a and b.
Note:	 If (a, b) are two distinct positive numbers and in, finding their HCF by Euclid’s 

division algorithm suppose first quotient is q and remainder is ‘r’, second quo-
tient is ‘q1’ and remainder is ‘r1’ third quotient is q2 and remainder is r2 and so 
on. If last divisor is rn when remainder become zero.

	 Then (rn) will be HCF of all pairs of numbers given below.
	 (rn) is HCF of (a, b), 
	 rn is also HCF of (b, r)
	 rn is also HCF of (r, r1)
	 rn is also HCF of (r1, r2)
	 (rn) is also HCF of (rn–2, rn–1) 

For making the understanding of concept of Euclid’s division algorithm. We take 
an example to find the HCF of 12156 and 37728.
Solution:

Step 1: We start with the larger integer 37728. By division algorithm, we get the relation 
37728 = 12156 × 3 + 1260
Step 2: Now, we consider the divisor 12156 as dividend and the remainder 1260 as 
divisor, by the application of division algorithm, we get the relation 
12156 = 1260 × 9 + 816
Step 3: Now, we consider the divisor 1260 as dividend and the remainder 816 as divisor, 
by the application of division algorithm, we get the relation   1260 = 816 × 1 + 444
Step 4: Now, consider the divisor 816 as dividend and the remainder 444 as divisor by 
the application of division algorithm, we get the relation   816 = 444 × 1 + 372
Step 5: Now, consider the divisor 444 as dividend and the remainder 372 as divisor 
by division algorithm, we get the relation 	
444	 = 372 × 1 + 72
Step 6: Now, consider the divisor 372 as dividend and the remainder 72 as divisor by 
division algorithm, we get the relation 	372	 = 72 × 5 + 12
Step 7: Now, consider the divisor 72 as dividend and the remainder 12 as divisor by 
division algorithm, we get the relation	72	= 12 × 6 + 0
Conclusion: As remainder in this step become zero hence HCF of: (37728, 12156) 
(12156, 1260) (1260, 816), (816, 444) (444, 372) (372, 72), (72, 12) is 12.
Hence HCF of 37728 and 12156 is 12.			   Ans. 12

Ex. 1.	 Find HCF of 231 and 396 using Euclid’s division algorithm.  	 [NCERT Exemplar]
Sol.	 We know that for finding the HCF of two distinct positive integers a and 

b (a > b) by using Euclid’s division algorithm we take larger number as ‘a’ 
and smaller number as ‘b’ and we obtain two integers q and r such that 
a = b × q + r, 0 ≤ r < b. 

	 This process remains continue till we get remainder as zero. [i.e. type of long division 
method] In this process when we get remainder as zero the last divisor is known 
as HCF. Now, for this particular question we take 396 as ‘a’ and 231 as ‘b’ and 396 
will express as under. 

	 Step (1):

	 Step(4): Remainder obtained in the step number (3) is 33 which is not zero so we

	 Finally we get remainder as zero hence HCF of 396 and 231 is 33 because last divisor

Ex. 4.	 Using Euclid’s division algorithm prove that : 847, 2160 are co-primes (relatively 
primes).			   [NCERT Exemplar]

Sol.	 Definition of co-primes or relatively primes: Two numbers are said to be co-prime 
or relatively prime. If their HCF is 1. Hence to prove 847 and 2160 as co-prime 
numbers we will find their HCF and which should be  1.

	 Now steps to find HCF will be as under 
				   2160	 = 847 × 2+ 466
				   847	 = 466 × 1 + 381
				   466	 = 381 × 1 + 85
				   381	 = 85 × 4 + 41
				   85	 = 41 × 2 + 3
				   41	 = 3 × 13 +  2
				   3	 = 2 × 1 + 1
				   2	 = 1 × 2 + 0
	 Therefore, the HCF  = 1. Hence, the numbers are co-primes (relatively prime). 
Ex. 5.	 If H is the HCF of 4052 and 12576 and H = 4052 × A + 12576 × B then find the value of 

[H + A + B].
Sol.	 Step 1: Since 12576 > 4052, we apply the division lemma to 12576 and 4052, we get
				   12576	 = 4052 × 3 + 420	 ...(1)
	 Step 2: Since the remainder 420 ≠ 0, we apply the division lemma to 4052 and 420, 

to get 
				   4052	 = 420 × 9 + 272	 ...(2)
	 Step 3: We consider the new divisor 420 and the new remainder 272, and apply 

the division lemma to get

Ex. 6.	 Find the largest number that divides 628, 3129 and 15630 to leave remainders 3, 4 
and 5 respectively. 

Sol.	 Required number 
			       = HCF of (628 – 3), (3129 – 4) and (15630 – 5) i.e., required number

			       = HCF of 625, 3125, 15625

	 To find HCF of 625, 3125 and 15625 first we will find HCF of 625 and 3125 and then 
we will find HCF of HCF of (625 & 3125) and 15625.

	 Step (1) : HCF of 625 and 3125 by using Euclid’s division algorithm is 

				   3125	 = 625 × 5 + 0

 	 ⇒	 HCF of 625 and 3125 is 625.
	 Step (2): Now HCF of 625 and 15625 will be :  15625 = 625 × 25 + 0
	 ⇒	 HCF of 625 and 15625 is 625.
	 Hence HCF of 625, 3125 and 15625 is 625. Hence, required number is 625.
Ex. 7.	 Find the largest number which divides 224, 250 and 302 and leaves remainder 3 in 

each case. 
Sol.	 Required number = HCF of (224 – 3), (250 – 3) and (302 – 3)
	 Required number is HCF of 221, 247 and 299.
	 Required number = HCF of 221 and 247 and then HCF of (221 & 247) and 299.
	 Step (1) HCF of 221 and 247 = 13 [by using Euclid’s division algorithm]
	 Step (2) HCF of 13 and 299 = 13 [By using Euclid’s division algorithm]
	 Hence HCF of 221, 247 and 299 is 13. Hence, required number is 13.

Ex. 8.	 Show that any positive odd integer is of the form 6q + 1 or 6q + 3 or 6q + 5, where 

q is some integer.			   [NCERT Textbook]

Sol.	 By Euclid division Algorithm, we have
				   a	 = bq + r     {0 ≤ r < b}	 ...(1)
	 On putting, b = 6 in equation (1), we get
				   a	 = 6q + r	 [0 ≤ r < 6 i.e., r = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

S chand Mathematics for Class X

	 If r = 0, a = 6q, 6q = 2 × 3q = 2m, where m = 3q is divisible by 2   ⇒   6q is even.
	 If r = 1, a = 6q + 1, 6q + 1 = 2 × 3q + 1 = 2m + 1, where m = 3q is not divisible by 2.
	 If r = 2, a = 6q + 2, 6q + 2 = 2 (3q + 1) = 2m, where m = (3q + 1) is divisible by 2 
		 ⇒   6q + 2 is even.
	 If r = 3, a = 6q + 3, 6q + 3 = 6q + 2 + 1 = 2 (3q + 1) + 1 = 2m + 1 where 
			  m = (3q + 1) is not divisible by 2.
	 If r = 4, a = 6q + 4, 6q + 4 = 2 (3q + 2) = 2m, where m = (3q + 2) is divisible by 2 
	 ⇒  6q + 4 is even.
	 If r = 5, a = 6q + 5, 6q + 5 = 6q + 4 + 1 = 2 (3q + 2) + 1 = 2m + 1, where m = (3q + 2) is not 

divisible by 2.
	 Since, 6q, 6q + 2, 6q + 4 are even.
	 Hence, the remaining integers 6q + 1, 6q + 3, 6q + 5 are odd.	 Proved.

Ex. 9.	 Use Euclid’s Division lemma to show that the square of any positive integer is 
either of the form 3m or 3m + 1 for some integer m.	 [NCERT Textbook]

Sol.	 By Euclid Division Algorithm, we have
				   a	 =  bq + r  [0 ≤ r < b]	 ...(1) 
	 On putting b = 3 in (1), we get
				   a	 = 3q + r,    [0 ≤ r < 3    i.e.,     r = 0, 1, 2]
	 If    r = 0 so, a = 3q           ⇒     a2 = 9q2 = 3 × (3q2) = 3m, where m = 3q2	 ...(2)
	 If    r = 1 so, a = 3q + 1     ⇒     a2 	= 9q2 + 6q + 1 = 3[3q2 + 2q] + 1 = 3m + 1,

	 If             r = 2 so, a = 3q + 2   ⇒   a2 = 9q2 + 12q + 4 = 9q2 + 12q + 3 + 1

	 From (2), 9q2 is a square of the form 3m, where m = 3q2

	 From (3), 9q2 + 6q + 1 i.e., 3 (3q2 + 2q) + 1 is a square which is of the form 
			     3m + 1 where m = 3q2 + 2q
	 From (4), 9q2 + 12q + 4 i.e., 3 (3q2 + 2q + 1) + 1 is a square which is of the form 

3m + 1, 
	 where m = 3q2 + 4q + 1. 
	 \ The square of any +ve integer is either of the form 3m or 3m + 1 for some 

integer m.    			   Proved.

Ex. 12.	 Show that the square of an odd positive integer can be of the form 6q + 1 or 6q +  3 

for some integer  q. 			   [NCERT Exemplar]

Sol.	 We know that any positive integer can be of the form 6m, 6m + 1, 6m + 2, 6m + 3, 
6m + 4 or  6m + 5, for some integer m. 

	 Thus, an odd positive integer can be of the form 6m +1, 6m + 3, or 6m + 5. 
	 Thus we have: 
	 (6m + 1)2 =  36 m2 + 12 m + 1 = 6 (6m2 + 2m) + 1 = 6q + 1, q = 6m2 + 2m is an integer. 
	 (6m + 3)2 =  36 m2 + 36 m + 9 = 6 (6m2 + 6m + 1) + 3 = 6q + 3, q = 6m2 + 6m + 1 is an 

integer.
	 (6m + 5)2 =  36 m2 + 60 m + 25 = 6 (6m2 + 10m + 4) + 1 = 6q + 1, q = 6m2 + 10m + 4 is 

an integer.
	 Thus, the square of an odd positive integer can be of the form 6q + 1 

or  6q + 3.

Ex. 13.	 Prove that one of any three consecutive positive integers must be divisible by 3.
[NCERT Exemplar]

Sol.	 Let three consecutive integers are m, m + 1, m + 2 where m ∈ N. 
	 Now we want to show that one and only one out of m, m + 1, m + 2 is divisible by  3.
	 As we want to show that one and only one out of m, m + 1, m + 2 is divisible by 3 

so let us take that any positive integer can be written in the form of 3q, 3q + 1, or 
3q +2 [here we are taking 3 as divisor so remainders can be 0, 1 or 2] 

	 Case I: When number is in the form of 3q then m, m + 1, and m + 2 will become 3q, 
3q+ 1, 3q + 2 by replacing (m) by 3q. Here it is very clear that only 3q is divisible by 
3. Hence proved in case  I. 

S chand Mathematics for Class X



10    S. Chand’s MATHEMATICS FOR CLASS X

	 Case II: If integer is in the form of (3q + 1) then numbers m, m + 1 and m + 2 will 
become 3q +  1, 3q + 2, 3q + 3 by replacing m by 3q + 1 as per condition of this case. 
Now it is clear that only last situation i.e. m + 2 become 3q + 3 which is only number 
divisible by 3. Hence, in this case also it is shown that only one of three consecutive 
numbers is divisible by 3.

	 Case III: If integer is in the form of (3q + 2), then numbers m, m + 1, m + 2 will be 
come 3q + 2, 3q + 3 , 3q + 4 by replacing each m by 3q + 2 as per condition of this 
case. Now, it is very clear that only in second situation i.e., m + 1 become 3q + 3 
which is multiple of 3. Hence in this case it is shown that one and only one out of 
three consecutive positive integers is divisible by 3.

Ex. 14.	 Prove that out of any two consecutive positive integers one and only one is even 
(i.e., multiple of 2).			   [NCERT Exemplar]

Sol.	 Let two consecutive positive integers are m and m + 1.
	 As we want to show that out of these two m and m + 1 one and only one is even i.e. 

multiple of 2 so we will take the statement that any positive integer can be written 
in the form of 2q or  2q + 1. Here divisor is 2 because we want to prove a number 
as even i.e. multiple of 2 so we have to take divisor as 2.

	 Now if divisor is 2 then there are only two cases possible one when remainder is 
zero and other when remainder is 1 because remainder has to be less than divisor 
i.e., 2 and greater or equal to zero. So only possible remainders are 0 and 1. Hence 
two cases are possible one when number is 2q + 0 and other when number is 2q  +  1.

	 Case I: When number is in the form of 2q then two consecutive positive integers 
m and m  +  1 become 2q and 2q + 1 by replacing m by 2q as per condition of this 
case. Now it is clear that m = 2q is multiple of 2 hence in this case m is multiple of 
2 and second m + 1 is not a multiple of 2. So one and only one number out of two 
consecutive positive integers is multiple of 2 or even. 

	 Case II: When number is in the form of 2q + 1 then two consecutive integers m and 
m + 1 will become 2q + 1 and 2q + 2 by replacing m by 2q + 1.

	 Now it is  clear that out of these two 2q + 1 and 2q + 2 only 2q + 2 is multiple of 2. 
Hence it is clear in this case that out of m and m + 1 only (m + 1) is even number. 
Hence one and only one out of two consecutive positive integers is even or divisible 
by 2.

Ex. 15. Prove that product of any three consecutive positive integers is always divisible 
by 6.				   [NCERT Exemplar]

Sol.	 From example 14 it is very clear that one out of two consecutive positive integers 
is always even i.e., multiple of 2. Now from example (13) it is also very clear that 
one and only one out of three consecutive positive integers is multiple of 3.

	 So from above discussion we can conclude that out of three consecutive positive 
integers one is surely multiple of 2 and one is surely multiple of 3 so obviously we 
can say that product of any three consecutive positive integer is divisible by the 
product of 2 and 3 i.e., 6.

Ex. 17.	 Prove that if x and y are odd positive integers, then x2 + y2 is even but not divisible 
by 4.				   [NCERT Exemplar]

Sol.	 We know that any odd positive integer is of the form 2q + 1 for some integer  q. 
	 So, let x = 2m + 1 and y = 2n + 1 for some integers m and n. 
	 \			   x2 + y2 	= 	(2m + 1)2 + (2n + 1)2   
	 ⇒			   x2 + y2 	= 	4(m2 + n2) + 4(m + n) + 2 
	 ⇒			   x2 + y2 	= 	4{(m2 + n2) + (m + n)} + 2
	 ⇒			   x2 + y2  	= 	4q + 2, where q = (m2 + n2) + (m + n)
	 ⇒	 x2 + y2 is even and leaves remainder 2 when divided by 4.
	 ⇒	 x2 + y2 is even but no divisible by 4.

Ex. 18.	 Show that n2 – 1 is divisible by 8, if n is an odd positive integer. 
[NCERT Exemplar]

Sol.	 We know that any odd positive integer is of the form 4m + 1 or 4m + 3 for some 
integer m. 

	 When      n = 4m + 1, then 
			  n2 – 1 = (4m + 1)2 – 1 = (16m2 + 8m + 1) – 1 = 16m2 + 8m = 8m (2m + 1)
	 ⇒	 n2 – 1 is divisible by 8.	[  8m (2m + 1) is divisible by 8]



	 When n = 4m + 3, then 
				   n2 – 1	 = (4m + 3)2 – 1 = (16m2 + 24m + 9) – 1
					    = 16m2 + 24m + 8 = 8(2m2 + 3m + 1)
	 ⇒	 n2 – 1 is divisible by 8.	[  8 (2m2 + 3m + 1) is divisible by 8]



	 Hence, n2 – 1 is divisible by 8.

Ex. 20.	 A sweetseller has 420 kaju barfis and 130 badam barfis. He wants to stack them in

stack and the number of stacks will then be the least. The area of the tray that is 
used up will be the least. 

	 Now, let us use Euclid’s algorithm to find their HCF. We have 
				   420	 = 130 × 3 + 30
				   130	 = 30 × 4 + 10
				   30	 = 10 × 3 + 0
	 So, the HCF of 420 and 130 is 10.
	 Therefore, the sweetseller can make stacks of 10 for both kinds of barfi.

CONCEPT – 2 : FUNDAMENTAL  THEOREM OF ARITHMETIC
Introduction:	 In general we have two types of numbers one prime numbers 

and other composite numbers.
Prime Numbers:	 Numbers which can not be divided by any number other 

than 1 and number itself are known as prime numbers for 
example 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23, ...etc. 

Composite Numbers:	 Numbers which can be divided by at least one of the number 
other than 1 and itself are known as composite numbers. 

Prime Factorisation of Composite Numbers
As discussed above that each composite number has at least one divisor other than 

one and number itself. So expressing the composite number as the product of all possible 
prime numbers is known as the prime factorisation of that composite number. 

Note:	Prime factorisation of different composite numbers are always different and for each com-
posite number its prime factors are unique.

Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
Statement 

Every composite number can be expressed (factorised) as a product of primes, and 
this factorisation is unique except for the order in which the prime factors are written. 

S chand Mathematics for Class X



NUMBER SYSTEM    17

For example prime factors of 30 can be written as : 
   30 = 2 × 3 × 5 = 2 × 5 × 3 = 3 × 5 × 2 = 3 × 2 × 5 = 5 × 2 × 3 = 5 × 3 × 2
So it is clear that prime factors of 30 can be written in 6 different forms but the prime 

numbers occurs in the prime factorisation of 30 are same in each case only their order is 
different but prime factorisation is unique which is only the conclusion given by fundamental 
theorem of Arithmetic. 

Explanation of fundamental theorem of Arithmetic with the help of factor tree 

Method to Find HCF and LCM of two or more numbers with the help of Fundamental 
theorem of Arithmetic 

Step 1:	 Find prime factorisation of all the numbers given of which HCF/LCM is 
required. 

Step 2:	 For finding HCF take the product of all common prime factors present in the 
prime factorisation of given numbers whose HCF is required. 

Step 3: 	 For finding LCM take the product of greatest powers of each prime factor 
available in the prime factorisation of given numbers. 

Applications of Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic 
1.	 We can find HCF of two or more numbers. 
2.	 We can find LCM of two or more numbers. 
3.	 If a and b are two distinct numbers and their HCF is ‘H’ and LCM is ‘L’
	 then a × b = H × L

Concept for finding the unit’s place digit in the given expansion 
	 1.	 If unit’s place digit of any number say ‘x’ is zero then the units place digit in 

the expansion of (x)n when n e N will always be zero. 
Or

		  We can say that expansion of any number (x)n can end with zero only if prime 
factors of base i.e. ‘x’ has at least one 2 and one 5 both if one 2 and one 5 is not 
available in the prime factors of base i.e. x then expansion of (x)n can not end 
with zero. 

	 2.	 If units place digit of a number say ‘x’ is 1 then units place digit in the expansion 
of (x)n when n ∈ N will always be 1.   

	 3.	 If unit’s place digit of a number say x is 2 then units place digit in the expansion 
of (x)n, n ∈ N will be 2 if n = 1, 4 if n = 2, 8 if n = 3, 6 if n = 4 and it is rule that 
after n = 4 unit’s place digits start repeating as under 
For n = 5 unit’s place digit will be same as for n = 1
For n = 6 unit’s place digit will be same as for n = 2
For n = 7 unit’s place digit will be same as for n = 3
For n = 8 unit’s place digit will be same as for n = 4 and this process remain to continue. 

	 4.	 If units place digit of a number say x is 3 then units place digit in the expansion 
of (x)n for n ∈ N will be : 3 if n = 1, 9 if n = 2, 7 if n = 3, 1 if n = 4 and after n = 4 
repetition of unit’s placed digit will start as per rule explained in point number 
3 for each value of n = 5 and above. 

	 5.	 If unit’s place digit of a number say x is 4 then unit’s place digit in the expansion 
of (x)n, n ∈ N will be 4 if n = 1, 6 if n = 2, 4 if n = 3, 6 if n = 4 i.e. for each odd 
‘n’, unit’s place digit will be 4 and for each even ‘n’, unit’s place digit will be 
even.

	 6.	 If unit’s place digit of a number say x is 5 then unit’s place digit in the expansion 
of (x)n, n ∈ N will always be 5.

	 7.	 If unit’s place digit in a number say x is 6, then unit’s place digit in the expansion 
of (x)n, n ∈ N will always be 6.

	 8.	 If unit’s place digit of a number say x is 7 then unit’s place digit in the expansion 
of (x)n, n ∈ N will be 7 if n = 1, 9 if n = 2, 3 if n = 3, 1 if n = 4 and usual repetition 
will be applicable for each value of n = 5 and above.

	 9.	 If unit’s place digit of a number say x is 8 then unit’s place digit in the expansion 
of (x)n, n ∈ N will be 8 if n = 1, 4 if n = 2, 2 if n = 3, 6 if n = 4 and usual repetition 
for any value of n = 5 and above. 

	 10.	 If unit’s place digit of a number say x is 9 then unit’s place digit in the expansion 
of (x)n, n ∈ N will be, 9 if n = 1, 1 if n = 2, 9 if n = 3, 1 if n = 4 and so on so we 
can conclude in this case that unit’s place digit will be 9 for any odd value of 
n and 1 for any even value of n.

Ex. 2.	 Find the LCM and HCF of 6 and 20 by the prime factorisation method. 
Sol.	 We have: 
		 6 = 21 × 31 and 20 = 2 × 2 × 5 = 22 × 51.
	 HCF (6, 20) = 21 = Product of the smallest power of each common prime factor in 

the numbers. 
	 LCM (6, 20) = 22 × 31 × 51 = Product of the greatest power of each prime factor, 

involved in the numbers. 
	 From this example we have noticed that HCF (6, 20) × LCM (6, 20) = 6 × 20 we can 

verify that for any two positive integers a and b, HCF (a, b) × LCM (a, b) = a × b. 
We can use this result to find the LCM of two positive integers, if we have already 
know the two positive integers and their HCF.

Ex. 7.	 Check whether expansion of (252)n, n ∈ N can end with zero for any n as natural

factorisation of base number i.e. x has at least one 2 and one 5 otherwise the 
expansion (x)n can never end with zero. 

	 Now to check whether (252)n can end with zero or not we will find the prime factors 
of base i.e. 252 which are as under 

			  252 	= 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 7 = 22 × 32 × 7   

	 The digit 5 does not appears in the prime factors of 252. 

	 Hence (252)n can never end with zero for any n ∈ N. 

Ex. 8.	 Check whether (75)n can end with zero for any n ∈ N.

factors of 75 hence for any n ∈ N (75)n cannot end with zero.

Ex. 9.	 Prove that there is no natural number for which 4n ends with the digit zero. 

[NCERT Textbook]

Sol.	 We know that any positive integer ending with the digit zero is divisible by 5 and 
so its prime factorisation must contain the prime 5.

	 We have, 

				   4n 	= (22)n = 22n 

	 ⇒	 The only prime in the factorisation of 4n is 2.

	 ⇒	 There is no other primes in the factorisation of 4n = 22n 

			  [By uniqueness of the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic]

	 ⇒	 5 does not occur in the prime factorisation of 4n for any national number  n. 

	 ⇒	 4n does not end with the digit zero for any natural number n. 

Ex. 10.	 Check whether 6n can end with the digit 0 or any n ∈ N.	 [NCERT Textbook]

Sol.	 If the number 6n ends with the digit zero. Then it is divisible by 5. Therefore the 
prime factorisation of 6n contains the prime 5. This is not possible because the only 
primes in the factorisation of 6n are 2 and 3 and the uniqueness of the fundamental 
theorem of arithmetic guarantees that there are no other prime in the factorisation 
of 6n.

	 So, there is no value of n in natural numbers for which 6n ends with the digit 
zero.				   Ans.

CONCEPT – 3 : REVISITING IRRATIONAL NUMBERS
Definition

p
	 1.	A number which can not be expressed in the form of  [where p & q are co-

q
primes (Relatively-prime)] and q ≠ 0 is known as on irrational numbers.

	 2.	A number which can not be expressed either terminating form or non-
terminating repeating form then it is known as irrational number. 

	 3.	Numbers in the form of non-terminating non repeating are known as irrational 
numbers. 

1
For example: 2 , 3 , ,  3.1020020002 ..........

2

Note:	 As we know that sum, difference, product and division of any two rational numbers 
is always rational (for division rational number in denominator should not be zero)

	 Similarly: Sum, difference, product and division of a rational number with an irrational 
is always results to an irrational number. 

Theorem 
Let p be a prime number. If p divides a2, then p divides a, where a is a positive integer.
Proof. Let P1, P2, P3 ... Pn be the factors of a. 
⇒	 a = P1. P2. P3 ... Pn, where P1, P2, .... are primes not necessarily all distinct.
Therefore 	a 2 = (P1. P2. P3 ... Pn) . (P1. P2. P3 .... Pn)

⇒	 a2 = P2 . P2 . P2 . . . 2
1 2 3 . . . . Pn

		  P divides a2	 ... (1)
⇒	 P is a prime factor of a2, from the fundamental theorem of Arithmetic. 
The prime factors of a2 are only            P1, P2, P3 .... Pn	 ... (2)

(Uniqueness of factors of Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic)
From (1) and (2), we have
P is a prime factors of P1. P2. P3 .... Pn
⇒	 	 P divides a.	 Proved.

CONCEPT – 4 : DECIMAL EXPANSION OF RATIONAL NUMBERS

TYPE – 1: Terminating Decimal Expansion
A rational number in the form of p/q with p and q co-primes q ≠ 0 can be expressed 

in the form of terminating decimal expansion if prime factors of denominator i.e. ‘q’ has 
either only 2m, only 5n or both 2m and 5n. For example  
	 1.	21/75 first it can be expressed in its simplest form i.e. 7/25, now prime factors 

of denominator i.e. 25 are 5 × 5. As prime factors of 25 has only 52 hence it is a 
terminating decimal expression but always remember first the number must be 
converted into the simplest form. Example (1):21/75 first converted into simplest 
form by writing 7/25 and then its denominator is factorized into its prime factors i.e., 
25 = 5 × 5. 

	 2.	63/64 clearly given rational number is in its simplest form hence we will find prime 
factors of denominator i.e. 64 hence 64 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 26. Clearly prime factors 
of 64 contains only 2s hence this rational number 63/64 can be expressed in the form 
of terminating decimal expansion. 

	 3.	33/1200, the simplest form of 33/1200 is 11/400, now prime factors of 400 are 2 × 2 × 
2 × 2 × 5 × 5 = 24 × 52. Clearly, prime factors of 400 contains four 2s and two 5s, hence 
it satisfy the condition of terminating decimal expansion so 33/1200 can be expressed 
in the form of terminating decimal expansion.

		 Conclusion: A rational number in the form of p/q (in its simplest form) can be 
expressed as terminating decimal expansion only if prime factors of denominators 
i.e. q is expressible in the form of 2m × 5n.   

TYPE – 2: Non-terminating Repeating Decimal Expansions

A rational number in the form of (p/q) (in its simplest form) can be expressed in the 
form of non-terminating repeating decimal expansion if its prime factors of denominator 
i.e. ‘q’ has any prime number in its prime factors other than 2s or 5s.
	 1.	If prime factors of denominator has 2s and some other number (other than 5s) 

then it is non-terminating repeating decimal expansion. 
	 2.	If prime factors of denominators i.e. q has 5s and some number other than 2s 

then also it can be expressed in the form of non-terminating repeating decimal 
expansion. 

	 3.	If prime factors of denominator has both 2s and 5s and some other prime number 
then also it will be expressed as non-terminating repeating decimal expansion. 

Ex. 1.	 29/600 clearly given rational number in its simplest form so now we will go to find 
the prime factors of its denominator

	 i.e.                   600 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 5 × 5 = 23 × 31 × 52.
	 As prime factors of denominator has three 2s, two fives and one 3  so we can 

conclude that as it has a number 3 in its prime factors other than 2s and 5s so it will 
be expressed as non-terminating repeating decimal expansion. 

S chand Mathematics for Class X



NUMBER SYSTEM    35

Ex. 2.	 57/162, the simplest form of 57/162 is 19/54. Now prime factors of denominator 54 
are 2 × 3 × 3 × 3. It has one 2 and three 3s so clearly it has prime number in its prime 
factors other than 2 so it will be expressed as non-terminating repeating decimal. 

Ex. 3.	 55/175, the simplest form of 55/175  is 11/35. Now prime factors of denominator 
35 are 35 = 5 × 7. Clearly prime factors of denominator has a prime number 7 other 
than 5 so its decimal expansion will expressed as non-terminating repeating decimal 
expansion.

		  Neither at n = – 1 and nor at 0 value of n2 – 1 is not divisible by 8. Hence n2 – 1 can not

T 	Sol.	 No, by Euclid’s lemma, b = aq + r, 0 ≤ r ≤ a. Here, b is any positive integer, a = 3, b = 3q + r

		  So, any positive integer is of the form 3k, 3k + 1 or 3k + 2

A 		  which is in the form of 3m and 3m + 1. Hence, square of any positive number cannot

	 5.	 A positive integer is of the form 3q + 1, q being a natural number. Can you write its

your answer.

S chand Mathematics for Class X



NUMBER SYSTEM    49

	Sol.	 No, by Euclid’s Lemma, b = aq + r, 0 ≤ r < a
		  Here, b is any positive integer a = 3, b = 3q + r for 0 ≤ r < 3 
		  So, this must be in the form 3q, 3q + 1 or 3q + 2
		  Now,       (3q)2 = 9q2 = 3m
		  and    (3q + 1)2 = 9q2 + 6q + 1 = 3(3q2 + 2q) + 1 = 3m + 1 [where, m = 3q2 + 2q]
		  Also, (3q + 2)2 = 9q2 + 12q + 4 = 9q2 + 12q + 3 + 1 = 3(3q2 + 4q + 1) + 1
			                     = 3m + 1			   [here, m = 3q2 + 4q + 1]
		  Hence, square of a positive integer is of the form 3q + 1 is always in the form 3m + 1 

for some integer m.
	 6.	 The numbers 525 and 3000 are both divisible only by 3, 5, 15, 25 and 75. What is HCF

	Sol.	 Since the HCF (525, 3000) = 75
		  By Euclid Lemma, 3000 = 525 × 5 + 375  [Q dividend = divisor × quotient + remainder]
				    525	= 375 × 1 + 150
				    375	= 150 × 2 + 75
				    150	= 75 × 2 = 0
		  and the numbers 3, 5, 15, 25 and 75 divides the numbers 525 and 3000 that mean these 

terms are common in both 525 and 3000. So, the highest common factor among these 
is 75.

2 Polynomials

TOPICS
1.	 Zeroes of a polynomial. 
2.	 Geometrical meaning of the zeroes of a polynomial. 
3.	 Relationship between zeroes and coefficients of a polynomial.
4.	 Division algorithm for polynomials. 

INTRODUCTION

	 1.	Polynomial: An algebraic expression in the form of a + a x1 + a x2
0 1 2 + ... + a .xn

n  where 
a0, a1, a2, … an are real numbers, n is a non-negative integer and an ≠ 0 is called a 
polynomial of degree n.

	 2.	Degree of Polynomial: The highest power of (variable) x in a polynomial p(x) is called 
the degree of polynomial. 

	 3.	Types of Polynomial:
	 (i)	 Constant polynomial: A polynomial of degree zero is called a constant 

polynomial and it is of the form P(x) = k.
	 (ii)	 Linear polynomial: A polynomial of degree one is called linear polynomial and 

it is of the form P(x) = ax + b, where a, b are real numbers and a ≠ 0.
	 (iii)	 Quadratic polynomial: A polynomial of degree two is called quadratic 

polynomial and it is of the form P(x) = ax2 + bx + c, where a, b, c are real numbers 
and a ≠0.

	 (iv)	 Cubic polynomial: A polynomial of degree three is called cubic polynomial and 
it is of the form P(x) = ax3 + bx2 + cx + d where a, b, c, d are real numbers and a 
≠ 0.

	 (v)	 Bi-quadratic polynomial: A polynomial of degree four is called Bi-quadratic 
polynomial or quadratic polynomial and it is of the form P(x) = ax4 + bx3 + cx2 + 
dx + e, where a, b, c, d, e are real numbers and a ≠ 0. 

Note:	 Number zero itself is known as zero polynomial and its degree is not defined because 
number zero can be written as 0 = 0 × 0 = 0 × x1 = 0 × x2 = 0 × x3 = 0 × x4 = 0 × x5 = … 
= 0 × xn = 0 × x∞.

56



POLYNOMIALS    57

	 (vi)	 Value of a polynomial: If p(x) is a polynomial in the form of : a0 + a1x + a2x
2 + 

a3x
3 + …+anxn with an ≠ 0, then value of the polynomial p(x) for a real value at 

x = a will be given by   P(a) = a0 + a1 × (a) + a2 × (a)2 + a3 × (a)3 + …..+ an × (a)n.  
	 (vii)	 Zero of a polynomial: A number ‘a’ is said to be the zero of a polynomial p(x), 

if on replacing each x in the polynomial by ‘a’ the value of polynomial comes 
out to be zero. 

CONCEPT – 1 : GEOMETRICAL MEANING OF ZEROES OF 
POLYNOMIAL

To make concept more interesting, more meaningful and more clear we can take the 
help of graphs for finding the zeroes of polynomial. As discussed in class IX that condition 
of a point to lie on x-axis is that its ordinate i.e. y must be zero. Hence any point of the form 
(K, 0) always lies on x-axis. 

Now if p(x) is any polynomial say a0 + a1x + a2x
2 + … + anxn, with an ≠ 0 of degree ‘n’ 

then by using trial and error method we can take (assume) few values of x which can make 
the value of polynomial p(x) as zero. 

Let us assume that if value of polynomial p(x) at x = k is zero then the co-ordinates of 
that point become (k, 0). Hence graph of the polynomial p(x) will cut or touch the x-axis at 
point (k, 0).

Hence x = k is its one of the zero. 
Now take it other way suppose the graph of a polynomial is given and it is meeting 

x-axis at (a, 0), (b, 0) and (0, 0) then each value of x i.e. abscissa where ordinate is zero is 
called zero of that polynomial. Hence, a, b and 0 are the zeroes of that polynomial whose 
graph meets x-axis at (a, 0), (b, 0)and (0, 0).
Note:
(1)	 Graph of a polynomial: p(x) does not meet x-axis any where it means 

the given polynomial does not has any real zeroes. 

(2) 	 If graph of any polynomial: p(x) meet the x-axis only at one point 
then it has only one zero and polynomial will be linear polynomial.

(3) 	 If graph of polynomial p(x) either cut the x-axis at 2 points or just touches the axis as shown 
in the figures then it has two real zeroes and polynomial is said to be quadratic polynomial.

(Continued)...

(4) If the graph of a polynomial p(x) intersects x-axis at three distinct points or intersects at 
one point also touches x-axis then the polynomial has 3 real zeroes and is said to be cubic 
polynomial. Possibilities are shown in the figure.

(5) A polynomial is said to has 4 real zeroes if the graph of the polynomial p(x): 

(i) Intersects x-axis at 4 points.

(ii) Intersects x-axis at 2 points and touches at one point.
(iii) Touches x-axis at 2 points.

(6) A constant polynomial say p(x) = k, k ≠ 0 does not has a real zero because we know that for

p(x) will never change it will remain only ‘k’. Also note that the value of p(x) is known as ‘y’ 
i.e. we always take p(x)  = y.

CONCEPT – 3 : PROBLEMS BASED UPON APPLICATION OF ZEROES
Some useful results based on zeroes (a and b) of a quadratic polynomial: 
1. a2 + b2 = (a + b)2 – 2ab = (α – β)2 + 2αβ
2. (a – b)2 = (a + b)2 – 4ab

3. α2 - β2 = (α + β)(α - β) = (α + β) (α + β)2 - 4αβ

4. a3 + b3 = (a + b)3 – 3ab(a + b)
5. a3 – b3 = (a – b)3 + 3ab(a – b)

CONCEPT – 4 : DIVISION ALGORITHM
Division algorithm for polynomials:

If p(x) and g(x) are any two polynomials with g(x) ≠ 0, then we can find polynomials 
q(x) and r(x) such that 

P(x)  = q(x)  × g(x) + r(x), where r(x) = 0 or degree of r(x) < degree of g(s).
Step 1. Divide the highest degree term of the dividend by the highest degree term of 

the divisor and obtain the remainder. 
Step 2. If the remainder is O or degree of remainder is less than divisor, then we 

cannot continue the division any further, if degree of remainder is equal to or more than 
divisor repeat step-1.

Ex. 4.	 Divide 3x2 – x3 – 3x + 5 by: x – 1 – x2. Also verify the division algorithm. 
[NCERT Textbook]

Sol.	 Note that the given polynomials are not in standard form. To carry out division, 
we first write both the dividend and divisor in decreasing orders of their powers. 

	 So, dividend	 =	 –x3 + 3x2 – 3x + 5 and divisor  = –x2 + x – 1. 
	 Division process is shown on the right side. 
	 We stop here since degree (3) = 0 < 1 = degree (–x2 + x – 1)
	 So, quotient	 =	 x – 2, remainder  = 3. 	    x – 2

	 Now, 	 Divisor × Quotient  + Remainder – x2 + x – 1	 – x3 + 3x2 – 3x + 5

				    =	 –x3 + x2 – x + 2x2 – 2x + 2 	+ 3   +	  –	   +
	        2x2 – 2x + 5

				    =	 –x3+  3x2 – 3x + 5
	        2x2 – 2x + 2

				    =	 Dividend 	           –	       +     –
	 In this way, the division algorithm is verified. 	                             3

	 Clearly, RHS of above result is divisible by the divisor.

the dividend, then it will be exactly divisible by the divisor. 
	 Dividing

Ex. 12.	 If two zeroes of the polynomial x4 – 6x3 – 26x2 + 138x – 35 are 2 ± 3 ,  find other

Sol.	 We have : 2 ± 3  are two zeroes of the polynomial
			   p(x) =x	 4 – 6x3 – 26x2 + 138x – 35
	 Let 		       x =	2 ± 3.  So, x – 2 = ± 3
	 Squaring, we get  	x2 – 4x + 4 = 3,  i.e.,  x2 – 4x + 1 = 0
	 Let us divide p(x) by x2 – 4x + 1 to obtain other zeroes.

						      x2 – 2x – 35

Ex. 14.	 Obtain all zeroes of polynomial p(x) = x3 + 13x2 + 32x + 20, if one of its zeroes is -2.
Sol.	 As (–2) is its one of zeroes so p(x) is divisible by (x + 2) so on dividing : x3 + 13x2 + 32x + 20 by 

(x + 2), we get 
		                      x + 2  x3 + 13x2 + 32x + 20  x2 + 11x + 10
	 Now, to find zeroes of x2 + 11x + 10 we can write x2 + 11x + 10 = (x + 10) (x + 1) 
	 ⇒ Zeroes are –1, –10
	 Hence, zeroes of x3 + 13x2 + 32x + 20 are
	 –2, –1 and –10.

INTRODUCTION
In IX class the students have learnt to solve linear equations in one variable. In this 

chapter we have to discuss linear equations in two variables.
In our daily life we come across many situations in which equations in two variables 

are required, such as,
Shivani went to Sunday market 

with her friends. They wanted to eat 
‘gol-gappa’ as well as “dahi-bhalla”. 
They took number of plates of “gol-
gappa” twice that of “dahi-bhalla”. 
The cost of one plate of gol-gappa was 
` 5 and cost of one plate of dahi-bhalla 
was ` 10. She spent ` 60 which she had 
spent for market. How would you find 
out the number of plates of “gol-gappa” 
and ‘‘dahi-bhalla’’ they took.

We will try to solve the problem with the help of linear equations in two variables. Let 
the number of plates of gol-gappa that Shivani and her friends took be x and the number 
of plates of dahi-bhalla they took be y.

		  x	 = 2y	 ...(1)

There are several ways to solve this pair of linear equations. 

Basic important concepts to understand
	 1.	Term: A Combination of 4 mathematical elements

	 (i)	 Sign ⊕ or !
	(ii)	 Number (any real number)
	(iii)	 Variable (a, b, c, x, y, z, p, a, r ...... etc)
	(iv)	 Exponents i.e. powers of variable
for example: 3x2 is a term because it has all 4 elements required for term i.e. sign ⊕ 

number 3, variable x, power 2.
7 1

		 Similarly 5y2, x, − y  are some examples of terms.

Note: All real numbers are known as constant term.

	 2.	Algebraic Expression: A combination of constant and variables, connected by four 
fundamental arithmetical operations of +, –, × and ÷ is called algebraic expression.

		 For example, 3 – 7x, 8 + 9y2, 6 – 7a + 8b are algebraic expressions.
		 Equation: An algebraic expression is equated to some constant, variable 

or other algebraic expression then that relation is known as equation, for 
example 3x + 7 = 10, x2 – 7x + 10 = 0, 9x – 7y = 10x + 12, xy + 7 = 20z.

		 Linear Equation: If the greatest exponent of the variable(s) in an equation is one, the 
equation is said to be a linear equation(s).

		 If the number of variables used in linear equation is one then equation is said to be 
linear equation in one variable.
For example, 3x + 11 = 0, 9y – 7 = 12, 6x – 12 = 18, 3t – 7 = 5 are some examples.
Linear equation in one variable is ax + b = 0 with a ≠ 0, and solution of this equation 

b
is the value of x which makes L.H.S. and R.H.S. equal. In the case of ax + b = 0, x = −  

a
is its solution.

	 	Linear equation in two variables: Equation of the form: ax + by + c = 0 with a ≠ 0, 
b ≠ 0 is known as linear equation in two variables. For example 3x – 2y – 1 = 0 or 
3x – 2y = 1, x + y = 2 or x + y – 2 = 0 are few examples of linear equations in two variables.
As discussed in class IX that graph of linear equation is a straight line so a linear 

equation in two variable has infinitely many solutions because graph of such equations is 

S chand Mathematics for Class X



110    S. Chand’s MATHEMATICS FOR CLASS X

a line and a line passes through infinitely many points and each point lies on line is known 
as its solution so a linear equation in two variables has infinitely many solutions.

Dependent and Independent Variable of a linear equation in two variables: It can 
be made very clear by taking an example of linear equation in two variables.
Let 3x + 2y = 5 is a linear equation in two variables so we can express x in terms of y 

5 − 2y
like: x =  then in this situation we assume our own the values of ‘y’ to get the 

3
values of x. Hence here y is known as independent variable because we are assuming 
the values of ‘y’. So value of x depends on the value of y assumed, hence ‘x’ is known 
as dependent variable.
Now for same linear equation in two variables  3x + 2y = 5.

5 − 3x
If y is expressed in the terms of x then y = .

2
In this situation we take (assume) value of x and for each value of x then value of y 
depend on the value of x assumed.
Hence in this situation x is independent variable and y is dependent variable.
So in a linear equation of type : ax + by = c (a ≠ 0, b ≠ 0). 
Case I If x is expressed in the terms of y then x is dependent variable and y is 

independent variable.
Case II If y is expressed in the terms of x then y is known as dependent variable and 
x is known as independent variable.
Solution: Solution is / are the value / values for the variable(s) used in equation which 
make(s) the two sides L.H.S. and R.H.S. of the equation equal.

System of Simultaneous Equations
Set of two linear equations in two variables written in the form of  a1x + b1y + c1 = 0, with 
a1 ≠ 0, b1 ≠ 0 and a2x + b2y + c2 = 0, with a2 ≠ 0, b2 ≠ 0 is known as system of simultaneous 
linear equations in two variables. 
To get solution of simultaneous linear equations in two variables two methods are used:
(i) Graphical method	 (ii)	 Algebraic method
If two or more pairs of values for x and y which satisfy the given equation are joined 
on graph paper, we find the graph of the given equation.
Every solution x = a, y = b (where a and b are real numbers), of the given equation 
determines a point (a, b) which lies on the graph of line.
Every point (c, d) lies on the line determines a solution x = c, y = d of the given equation. 
Thus, line is known as the graph of the given equation.

  (i)  The graph of x = constant is a line parallel to the y-axis.
 (ii) The graph of y = constant is a line parallel to the x-axis.
(iii) The graph of y = x & y = – x passes through origin.
By finding common solutions of two (more) equations we mean a pair of value required 

one for x and other for y, which satisfy both the equations simultaneously.
There are three possibilities of two given lines in a plane :
	 (i)	 When the lines are intersecting: If the lines are intersecting, the equations are 

consistent and there exist a unique solution, and the point of intersection gives 
the unique solution (common solution).

	(ii)	 When the lines are parallel: If the lines are parallel, we have no solution and system 
is said to be inconsistent.

	(iii)	 When the lines are coincident: If both the equations are represented by same 
line then the two given equations are said to be dependent equations. In this case, 
there are infinite solutions.

Consistency and Inconsistency of system of simultaneous linear equations 
(Algebraically)

For system of simultaneous linear equations in two variables:
	  a1x + b1y + c1 = 0, a1 ≠ 0, b1 ≠ 0 and  a2x + b2y + c2 = 0, a2 ≠ 0, b2 ≠ 0

	 1.	If graphs of two lines intersects then system is said to be consistent with unique solution.
	 2.	If graphs of two lines are parallel then system is said to be in consistent or no common 

solution.
	 3.	If graphs of two lines are concident then system is known as consistent with infinite 

solution.
Now if we want to check their conditions of consistency or inconsistency without 

plotting the graphs then we check the following conditions.

Ex. 11.	 Half the perimeter of rectangular garden, whose length is 4 m more than its width, 

is 36 m. Find the dimensions of the garden.	 [NCERT Textbook]
Sol.	 Let the length of the garden be x m and 

its width be y m.
	 Then, perimeter  = 2(Length + Width) 
				   = 2(x + y)
	 Therefore, 	 half perimeter 	= (x + y)
	 But it is given as 36
	 ∴	      (x + y) = 36		                ...(1)
	 Also,     x	= y + 4, i.e., x – y = 4           ...(2)
	 For finding the solution of (1) and (2) 

graphically, we form the following table :

		 x + y = 36	 x – y = 4
x 20 24 x 10 16
y 16 12 y 6 12

	 Draw the graphs by joining points (20, 16) and (24, 12) and points (10, 6) and 
(16, 12). The two lines intersect at point (20, 16) as shown in the graph.

	 Hence, Length = 20 m and width = 16 m.	 Ans.

CONCEPT–2 : SOLUTION OF SYSTEM OF SIMULTANEOUS LINEAR 
                          EQUATIONS ALGEBRAICALLY

TYPE – 1: Substitution Method

Algebraic solution of a system of linear equations
Sometimes, graphical method does not give an accurate answer. While reading the 

coordinates of a point on a graph paper, we are likely to make an error. So, we require some 
precise method to obtain accurate result. Algebraic methods given below yield accurate 
answers.
	 (i)	 Method of elimination by substitution.
	 (ii)	 Method of elimination by equating the coefficients.
	 (iii)	 Method of cross multiplication.

Substitution Method
In this method, we first find the value of one variable (y) in terms of another variable 

(x) from one equation. Substitute this value of y in the second equation. Second equation 
becomes a linear equation in x only and it can be solved for x.

S chand Mathematics for Class X

3x
–

y =
2



PAIR OF LINEAR EQUATIONS IN TWO VARIABLES    125

Putting the value of x in the first equation, we can find the value of y.
This method of solving a system of linear equations is known as the method of elimination 

by substitution. 
‘Elimination’, because we get rid of y or ‘eliminate’ y from the second equation. 

‘Substitution’, because we ‘substitute’ the value of y in the second equation.

Working Rule :
Let the two equations be
		   a1x + b1y + c1 =	 0	 ...(1)
		  a2 x + b2y + c2 =	 0	 ...(2)
Step 1.	 Find the value of one variable, say y, in terms of the other i.e. x from any 

equation, say (1).
Step 2.	 Substitute the value of y obtained in step 1 in the other equation i.e. equation 

(2). This equation becomes equation in one variable x only.
Step 3.	 Solve the equation obtained in step 2 to get the value of x.
Step 4.	 Substitute the value of x from step 3 to the equation obtained in step 1. From 

this equation, we get the value of y. In this way, we get the solution i.e. values 
of x and y.

Remark : Verification is a must to check the answer.

SOLVED EXAMPLES

(substitution)
				   2x – 3y =	 7

TYPE – 2: Elimination Method

Method of elimination by equating the coefficients
In this method, the coefficients of any one variable ‘y’ in both the equations are 

made equal by multiplying the equations with the suitable non-zero number. By adding/
subtracting one of the two variables (y) is eliminated to get an equation in one variable x. 
The equation obtained in one variable (x) is solved to get the value of the variable (x). The 
value of this variable (x) is substituted in any of the equation to get the value of the other 
variable (y). In this method, multiplication is used instead of division. Multiplication 
is more convenient than division. So this method is preferred than the previous one.

Working Rule
Let the two equations be
		     a1x + b1y + c1 =	 0                                  ...(1)
		   a2x + b2y + c2 =	 0	 ...(2)

S chand Mathematics for Class X



PAIR OF LINEAR EQUATIONS IN TWO VARIABLES    133

Step 1.	 To eliminate y, multiply equation (1) by b2 and equation (2) by b1.
			   [To eliminate x, multiply equation (1) by a2 and equation (2) by a1].
Step 2.	 Subtract the equations obtained in step 2. The variable y is eliminated and 

we get an equation in one variable x.
Step 3.	 Solve the equation in one variable (x) obtained in step 2.
Step 4.	 Substitute the value of one unknown (x), found in step 3 in any one of the 

given equations.
Step 5.	 Solve the equation obtained in step 4 and get the value of the other unknown 

(y). In this way, we get the solution i.e. values of x and y.

SOLVED EXAMPLES

TYPE – 3: Examples based on method of Cross-multiplication

Cross-multiplication Method
By the method of elimination by substitution, only those equations can be solved, which 

have unique solution. But the method of cross multiplication discussed below is applicable 
in all the cases; whether the system has a unique solution, no solution or infinitely many 
solutions.

Let us solve the following system of equations
		  a1x + b1y + c1 =	 0	 ...(1)
		  a2x + b2y + c2 =	 0	 ...(2)
Multiplying equation (1) by b2 and equation (2) by b1, we get
		  a1b2 x + b1b2 y + b2c1 =	 0	 ...(3)
		  a2b1 x + b1b2 y + b1 c2 =	 0	 ...(4)
Subtracting equation (4) from equation (3), we get
		  (a1b2 – a2 b1) x + (b2 c1 – b1 c2) =	 0

CONCEPT–3 : CONDITIONS FOR CONSISTENCY OR SOLVABILITY
Let 		  a1x + b 1 y + c1 =	 0	 ...(1)
		  a2x + b2 y + c2 =	 0	 ...(2)
Multiplying the equation (1) by b2 and equation (2) by b1, we get
		  a1b2x + b1b2 y + b2c1 =	 0	 ...(3)
		  a2b1x + b1b2 y + b1c2 =	 0	 ...(4)
Subtracting equation (4) from equation (3), we get
		  x (a1 b2 – a2 b1) =	 b1c2 – b2c1	 ...(5)
Similarly,	 y (a1 b2 – a2b1) =	 c1a2 – c2a1	 ...(6)

Ex. 1.	 7 audio cassettes and 3 video cassettes cost ` 1110, while 5 audio cassettes and 4 
video cassettes cost ̀  1350. Find the cost of an audio cassette and a video cassette.

Sol.	 Let the cost of an audio cassette be ` x and that of a video cassette be ` y.
	 Then,	 7x + 3y =	 1110	 ...(1)
	 and		   5x + 4y =	 1350	 ...(2)
	 Multiplying equation (1) by 4 and equation (2) by 3, we get
				   28x + 12y =	 4440	 ...(3)
				    15x + 12y =	 4050	 ...(4)
	 Subtracting (4) from (3), we have
				    13x =	 390	 ⇒	 x = 30

S chand Mathematics for Class X



172    S. Chand’s MATHEMATICS FOR CLASS X

	 On putting x = 30 in equation (1), we get
				     7 × 30 + 3y =	 1110	 ⇒	 3y = 1110 – 210 = 900
	 ⇒			   y =	 300
	 Hence, the cost of an audio cassette = x = ` 30
	 and the cost of a video cassette = y = ` 300	 Ans.

Ex. 2.	 Two numbers differ by 3 and their product is 54. Find the numbers.	
Sol.	 Let the two numbers be x and y. According to the 1st condition,
	 Difference of the two numbers = 3
	 ⇒	 	 x – y =	 3
	 ⇒		  y =	 x – 3	 ...(1)
	 According to second condition, Product of two numbers = 54
	 ⇒		  xy =	 54	 ...(2)
	 Substituting  y = x – 3 from (1) in (2), we get
				    x (x – 3) =	 54	 ⇒	 x2 – 3x = 54
	 ⇒			   x2 – 3x – 54 =	 0	 ⇒	 x2 – 9x + 6x – 54 = 0
	 ⇒			   x (x – 9) + 6 (x – 9) =	 0	 ⇒	 (x – 9) (x + 6) = 0
	 ⇒			   x =	 9 and x = – 6
	 On putting x = 9 in equation (1), we have
				   y =	 9 – 3 = 6
	 On putting x = –6 in (1), we get y = – 6 – 3 = – 9
	 Hence, the numbers are 9 and 6 or –9 and –6.	 Ans.

Ex. 7.	 The sum of a two digit number and the number obtained by reversing the order of

Ex. 18.	 A train covered a certain distance at a uniform speed. If the train would have been 
10 km/h faster, it would have taken 2 hours less than the scheduled time. And if the 
train were slower by 10 km/h, it would have taken 3 hours more than the scheduled 
time. Find the distance covered by the train.		                      [NCERT Textbook]

Sol.	 Let the original speed of the train be x km/h and let the time taken to complete the 
journey be y hours.

	 Then,	the distance covered = xy km
	 Case I: When	 speed =	 (x + 10) km/h
	 and		  time taken =	 (y – 2) hour
	 In this case,	 distance =	 (x + 10) (y – 2)
	 ⇒		  xy =	 (x + 10) (y – 2)
	 ⇒		  xy =	 xy – 2x + 10y – 20
	 ⇒		  2x – 10y + 20 =	 0	 ...(1)
	 Case II:  When	 speed =	 (x – 10) km/h
	 and		  time taken =	 (y + 3) hour
	 In this case,	 distance =	 (x – 10)(y + 3)
	 ⇒		  xy =	 (x – 10)(y + 3)
	 ⇒		  xy =	 xy + 3x – 10y – 30	 ...(2)
	 ⇒		  3x – 10y – 30 =	 0
	 Subtracting (1) from (2), we get
				   x – 50 =	 0  ⇒  x = 50
	 Putting x = 50 in (1), we get
				   100 – 10y + 20 =	 0  ⇒  – 10y = – 120
	 or		  y =	 12
	 ∴	 The original speed of the train = 50 km/h
		 The time taken to complete the journey = 12 hours
	 Hence, the length of the journey = Speed × Time = (50 × 12) km = 600 km

Ex. 19.	 The students of a class are made to stand in rows. If 3 students are extra in a row, 
there would be 1 row less. If 3 students are less in a row, there would be 2 rows 
more. Find the number of students in the class.	 [NCERT Textbook]

Sol.	 Let originally there be x students in each row. Let there be y rows in total. Therefore, 
total number of students is xy.

	 Case I: When 3 students are taken extra in each row, then the number of rows 
in this case becomes (y – 1).

	 	∴	 	 xy =	 (x + 3)(y – 1)
		 ⇒		  xy =	 xy – x + 3y – 3
		 ⇒		  x – 3y + 3 =	 0	 ...(1)
	 Case II: When 3 students are taken less in each row, then the number of rows 

becomes (y + 2).
		 ∴	 	 xy =	 (x – 3)(y + 2)
		 ⇒		  xy =	 xy + 2x – 3y – 6
		 ⇒		  2x – 3y – 6 =	 0	 ...(2)
		 Solving (1) and (2), we get
				   x =	 9,  y = 4
		 Hence, 	the number of students = xy = 9 × 4 = 36.

	 1.	 The sum of the digits of a two digit number is 8 and the difference between the number 

and that formed by reversing the digits is 18. Find the number.
	 2.	 A train covered a certain distance at a uniform speed. If the train would have been 

6 km/hr. faster, it would have taken 4 hours less than the scheduled time. And if the 
train were slower by 6 km/hr., it would have taken 6 hours more than the scheduled 
time. Find the length of the journey.

	 3.	 Ratio between the girls and boys in a class of 40 students is 2 : 3. Five new students 
joined the class. How many of them must be boys so that the ratio between girls and 
boys becomes 4 : 5?

	 4.	 If you travel by an autorickshaw the fare for the first kilometre is different from the 
rate per km for the remaining distance. The total fare for a distance of 20 km is ` 37.70 
and that for a distance of 26 km is ̀  48.50. Find the auto fare for the first kilometre and 
for each successive kilometre.

	 5.	 One kilogram of tea and 4 kg of sugar together cost ̀  220. If the price of sugar increases 
by 50% and the price of tea increases by 10% the cost would be ̀  266. Find the original 
cost per kilogram of each.

	 6.	 A man bought 4 horses and 9 cows for ` 1340. He sells the horses at a profit of 10% 
and the cows at a profit of 20% and his whole gain is ` 188. What price did he pay for 
the horse?

	 7.	 The largest angle of a triangle is equal to the sum of the other two angles. The smallest 
angle is 1/4 of the largest angle. Find the angles of the triangle.

	 8.	 A man when asked how many hens and buffaloes he has told that his animals have 
120 eyes and 180 legs. How many hens and buffaloes has he?

	 9.	 The sum of a two digit number and the number obtained by reversing the order of its 
digits is 121 and the two digits differ by 3. Find the number.

	 10.	 A railway half ticket costs half the full fare and the reservation charge is the same on 
half ticket as on full ticket. One reserved first class ticket from Bombay to Ahmedabad 
costs ` 216 and one full and one half reserved first class tickets cost ` 327. What is the 
basic first class full fare and what is the reservation charge?

	 11.	 A fraction becomes 4/5 if 1 is added to both numerator and denominator. If however 
5 is subtracted from both numerator and denominator, the fraction becomes 1/2. What 
is the fraction?

	 12.	 Seven times a two digit number is equal to four times the number obtained by reversing 
the order of digits, and the sum of the digits of the number is 3. Find the number.

	 13.	 A two digit number is obtained by either multiplying sum of the digits by 8 and adding 
1 or by multiplying the difference of the digits by 13 and adding 2. Find the number.

	 14.	 3 chairs and 2 tables cost ` 700 and 5 chairs and 3 tables cost ` 1100. What is the cost 
of 2 chairs and 2 tables?

	 15.	 Points A and B are 70 km apart on a highway. A car starts from A and another car 
starts from B at the same time. If they travel in the same direction, they meet in 7 hrs. 
but if they travel towards each other they meet, in one hour. What are their speeds?

	 19.	 A man walks a certain distance with certain speed. If he walks 1/2 km/hr. faster,

	 20.	 The incomes of X and Y are in the ratio of 8 : 7 and their expenditures are in the ratio

	 22.	 A motor boat can travel 30 km upstream and 28 km downstream in 7 hours. It can

	 13.	 Write an equation of a line passing through the point representing solution of the pair 

of linear equations x + y = 2 and 2x – y = 1. How many such lines can we find?
 	Sol.	 First we will find the coordinates of point i.e., values of x and y from equations: 

x + y = 2 and 2x – y = 1
			   x + y =	2	 (1)
			   2x – y =	1	 (2)
		  on solving equation (1) and (2) we get x = 1 and y = 1
		  Now we can write infinite number of equations passing through the point whose 

coordinates are given by x = 1 and y =1.
		  for example x – y = 0,  2x + y = 3,  x + 2y = 3 etc.
		  Note: As we can draw infinite number of lines passing through a point so we can write 

infinite number of equations passing through any point.

	19.	 There are some students in the two examination halls A and B. To make the number 

of students equal in each hall, 10 students are sent from A to B. But if 20 students are 
sent from B to A, the number of students in A becomes double the number of students 
in B. Find the number of students in the two halls.

	Sol.	 Let the number of students in halls A and B are x and y, respectively.
		  Now, by given condition,	 x – 10 =	y + 10
		  ⇒	 x – y =	20	 ...(1)
		  and	 (x + 20) =	2(y – 20)
		  ⇒	 x – 2y =	– 60	 ...(2)
		  On substracting Eq. (ii) from Eq. (i), we get
			   (x – y) – (x – 2y) =	20 + 60
			   x – y – x + 2y =	80  ⇒  y = 80
		  On putting y = 80 in Eq. (1), we get
			   x – 80 =	20  ⇒  x = 100 and y = 80
		  Hence, 100 students are in hall A and 80 students are in hall B.

	22.	 The angles of a cyclic quadrilateral ABCD are 
		  ∠A = (6x + 10)°,	 ∠B =	 (5x)°
		  ∠C = (x + y)°,	 ∠D =	 (3y – 10)°
		  Find x and y, and hence the values of the four angles.	
	Sol.	 We know that, by property of cyclic quadrilateral,
		  Sum of opposite angles = 180°
			   ∠A + ∠C =	(6x + 10)° + (x + y)° = 180°
					    [... ∠A = (6x + 10)°, ∠C = (x + y)°, given]
		  ⇒	 7x + y =	170	 ...(1)
		  and	 ∠B + ∠D =	(5x)° + (3y – 10)° = 180°
					    [... ∠B = (5x)°, ∠D = (3y – 10)°, given]
		  ⇒	 5x + 3y =	190°	 ...(2)
		  On multiplying Eq. (1) by 3 and then subtracting, we get
			   6 × (7x + y) – (5x + 3y) =	510° – 190°
		  ⇒	 21x + 3y – 5x – 3y =	320°  ⇒  16x = 320°
		  ∴	 x =	20°
		  On putting x = 20° in Eq. (1), we get

N 			   7 × 20 + y =	170°
		  ⇒	 y =	170° – 140°  ⇒  y = 30°

C 		  ∴	 .∠A =	(6x + 10°) = 6 × 20° + 10°
E 			    =	120° + 10° =130°
R 			   ∠B =	(5x)° = 5 × 20° = 100°
T 			   ∠C =	(x + y)° = 20° + 30° = 50°

			   ∠D =	(3y – 10)° = 3 × 30° – 10° = 90° – 10° = 80°

E 		  Hence, the required values of x and y are 20° and 30° respectively and the values of 
the four angles i.e., ∠A, ∠B, ∠C and ∠D are 130°, 100°, 50° and 80° respectively.

Quadratic Equations

TOPICS

1.	 Quadratic equations		  2.  Roots of a quadratic equation
3.	 Solutions of quadratic equation
	 (a) By the method of factorization
	 (b) By the method of completing the square or Sridharacharya Rule/Method
	 (c) By the quadratic formula
4.	 Nature of roots
5.	 Relation between roots of quadratic equations and their coefficients.

INTRODUCTION 
If p(x) is a quadratic polynomial, then p(x) = 0 is called a quadratic equation. For example, 
x2 + 2x – 8 =  0, x2 – 5x + 6 = 0 are quadratic equations. The general form of a quadratic 
equation is ax2 + bx + c = 0, where a, b, c ∈ R and a ≠ 0.

Many a times, such equations 
come up, while dealing with real life 
situations. For example in Rasika’s 
school, all the students come to ground 
for morning prayer before the teaching 
period. All the students of a class stand 
in one row. If the number of students 
is 495. If the number of columns in this 
assembly is three more than twice the 
number of rows. What is the number 
of rows and columns in this assembly?

Suppose, the number of rows = x
The number of the columns = 2x + 3
Total number of students = 495
Total number of the students = x(2x + 3)
⇒	 495	 = x(2x + 3)  ⇒  495 = 2x2 + 3x
⇒		  2x2 + 3x – 495	 = 0

242



QUADRATIC EQUATIONS    243

On solving the equation we can find out the number of rows and number of columns.
Brahmagupta (598 – 665 A.D.) gave an explicit formula to solve a quadratic equation 

of the form ax2 + bx + c = 0. The next Indian mathematician Sridharacharya (1025 A.D.) 
gave the method of derivation of this formula, now known as quadratic formula as quoted 
by Bhaskara II.

In this chapter we will study quadratic equations and various methods of solving them.

CONCEPT – 1 : QUADRATIC EQUATIONS
(a)	 STANDARD FORM OF QUADRATIC EQUATION

The equation of the form ax2 + bx + c = 0, a ≠ 0 is known as standard quadratic equation. 
For example,
 5x2 + 3x + 6 = 0 is a quadratic equation in the standard form.

(b)	 ROOTS OF A QUADRATIC EQUATION
If p(x) = 0 is a quadratic equation, then the zeroes of the polynomial p(x) are called the 

roots of the quadratic equation p(x) = 0.
Thus, x = 1 is a root of p(x) = x2 + x – 2 = 0, since p(1) = (1)2 + 1 – 2 = 0
	    x = –2 is also a root of x2 + x – 2 = 0, since p(– 2) = (– 2)2 + (– 2) – 2 = 4 – 2 – 2 = 0

Notes .	 1.	x = a is a root of p(x) = 0, iff p(a) = 0.
	 2. 	Every quadratic equation can have at most two real roots.
	 3.	Finding the roots of a quadratic equation is known as solving the quadratic equation.

(c)	 WORKING RULE TO EXAMINE WHETHER THE GIVEN EQUATION IS 
QUADRATIC OR NOT.
Step 1. Write down the given equation in the form f(x) = 0
Step 2. (a) If f(x) is a polynomial, then observe its degree.
       (b) If f(x) is not a polynomial, then first make it polynomial and then observe 

its degree.
Step 3. If degree of the polynomial is 2, then the given equation is quadratic.

Ex. 4.	 Represent the following situations in the form of quadratic equations:
	 (i)	 The area of a rectangular plot is 528 m2. The length of the plot (in metres) is 

one more than twice its breadth. We need to find the length and breadth of 
the plot.

	 (ii)	 The product of two consecutive positive integers is 306. We need to find the 
integers.

	 (iii)	 Rohan’s mother is 26 years older than him. The product of their ages, 3 years 
from now will be 360. We would like to find Rohan’s present age.

	 (iv)	 A train travels a distance of 480 km at a uniform speed. If the speed had been 
8 km/h less, then it would have taken 3 hours more to cover the same distance. 
We need to find the speed of the train.	 [NCERT Textbook]

Sol.	 (i)   Let the breadth of the plot be x metres.
			  Then the length of the plot is one more than twice its breadth, i.e., (2x + 1) 

metres
			  Area of the plot = 528 m2

			  Length × Breadth = Area of the Plot
			  ⇒	 (2x + 1)x	 = 528
			  ⇒	 2x2 + x	 = 528
			  ⇒	 2x2 + x – 528	 = 0
			  This is the required quadratic equation.
	 (ii)	 Let the two consecutive positive integers be x and x + 1. Then, according to 

the question:
			  x(x + 1)	= 306  ⇒  x2 + x – 306 = 0
			  This is the required equation.
	 (iii)	 Let the age of Rohan be x years. 
			  Then his mother’s age is (x + 26) years
			  After three years:
			  Rohan’s age = (x + 3) years
			  Rohan’s mother’s age = (x + 26) + 3 years = (x + 29) years
			  According to the question.
				   (x + 3) (x + 29)	 = 360
			  ⇒	 x2 + 29x + 3x + 87	 = 360  ⇒  x2 + 32x – 273 = 0.
		 	 Therefore, the age of Rohan satisfies the quadratic equation x2 + 32x – 273 = 0.
	 (iv)	 Distance travelled by the train = 480 km
		  Let the speed of train = x km/h
		  It is given the time to cover 480 km is increased by 3 hours if the train’s speed 

is reduced by 8 km/hr.
480 480

x − 8 x

CONCEPT – 4 : NATURE OF THE ROOTS

Let the quadratic equation be ax2 + bx + c = 0.  Then

−b ± b2 − 4ac
	 	 x = 

2a
So, a quadratic equation ax2 + bx + c = 0

	 (i)	 has no real roots if b2 – 4ac < 0,
	 (ii)	 has two equal real roots if b2 – 4ac = 0,
	 (iii)	 has two distinct real roots if b2 – 4ac > 0.
	 (iv)	 has real roots if b2 – 4ac ≥ 0.

Note. Discriminant b2 – 4ac is denoted by D.

SOLVED EXAMPLES

	   (i)	 x2 – 4x + 3 = 0	 (ii)	 3x2 – 5x – 2 = 0	 (iii)	 6x2 + x – 2 = 0

Sol.	 (i)	 The given quadratic equation is x2 – 4x + 3 = 0.
			  Hence, clearly a = 1, b = – 4 and c = 3
	  		  D	 = b2 – 4ac = (– 4)2 – 4 × 1 × 3 = 16 – 12 = 4
	 (ii)	 The given quadratic equation is 3x2 – 5x – 2 = 0

Ex. 2.	 Examine, whether the following equations have real roots:	
	 (i)	 x2 + x + 1 = 0	 (ii) 3x2 + 2x – 1 = 0	  (iii) 2x2 + 5x + 5 = 0
	 (iv)	 x2 + 4x + 4 = 0	 (v) 2x2 + x – 1 = 0	 (vi) x2 + 5x + 5 = 0
Sol.	 (i)	 x2 + x + 1 = 0
			  Here, a = 1, b = 1, c = 1   (Comparing the given equation with ax2 + bx + c = 0)
	 		 Therefore, discriminant D = b2 – 4ac = (1)2 – 4(1) (1) = – 3 < 0
			  Since D < 0, the equation has no real roots.
	 (ii)		  3x2 + 2x – 1	 = 0
			  Here,  a = 3, b	= 2, c = –1	(Comparing the given equation with ax2 + bx + c = 0)
			  Therefore, discriminant D = b2 – 4ac = (2)2 – 4(3)(–1) = 4 + 12 = 16 > 0
			  Since D > 0, the equation has real roots.
	 (iii)		  2x2 + 5x + 5	 = 0
			  Here,      a = 2, b = 5, c = 5
			  Therefore, discriminant D = b2 – 4ac = (5)2 – 4(2)(5) = 25 – 40 = – 15 < 0
			  Since D < 0, the equation has no real roots.
	 (iv)	 	 x2 + 4x + 4	 = 0
			  Here, a = 1, b = 4, c = 4
			  Therefore, discriminant D = b2 – 4ac = (4)2 – 4(1)(4) = 16 – 16 = 0
			  Since D = 0, the equation has equal real roots.
	 (v)		  2x2 + x – 1	 = 0
			  Here, a = 2, b = 1, c = – 1
			  Therefore, discriminant D = b2 – 4ac = (1)2 – 4(2)(–1) = 1 + 8 = 9 > 0
			  Since D > 0, the equation has real roots.
	 (vi)	 		  x2 + 5x + 5 = 0
			  Here, a = 1, b = 5, c = 5
			  Therefore, discriminant D = b2 – 4ac = 52 – 4(1)(5) = 25 – 20 = 5 > 0
			  Since D > 0, the equation has real roots.

Ex. 10.	 Find the values of k for which of the following equation has equal roots:
			  (k – 12) x2 + 2 (k – 12) x + 2 = 0
Sol.	 We have,
			         (k – 12) x2 + 2 (k – 12) x + 2 = 0
	 Here,	 a =	 k – 12, b = 2 (k – 12) and c = 2
	 ∴		   D =	 b2 – 4ac = 4 (k – 12)2 – 4 (k – 12) × 2
	 ⇒		  D =	 4 (k – 12) {(k – 12) – 2}
	 ⇒		  D =	 4 (k – 12) (k – 14)
	 The given equation will have equal roots, if
	 D = 0 ⇒ 4 (k – 12) (k – 14) = 0 ⇒ k – 12 = 0 or, k – 14 = 0 ⇒ k = 12 or, k = 14
	 But k = 12 is not possible because at k = 12 given equation will not be quadratic it 

will become linear equation hence Answer is k = 14.

Ex. 13.	 Show that the equation x2 + ax – 4 = 0 has real and distinct roots for all real values 

of a.
Sol.	 The given equation is x2 + ax – 4 = 0
	 The discriminant of the given equation is given by D = a2 – 4 × – 4 = a2 + 16
	 Clearly,  D = a2 + 16 > 0 for all a ∈ R.
	 Hence, the given equation has real and distinct roots.

Ex. 15.	 Determine the positive values of ‘k’ for which the equation x2 + kx + 64 = 0 and 

x2 – 8x + k = 0 will both have real roots.
Sol.	 Given equations are
				   x2 + kx + 64 =	 0	 …(1)
	 and,		 x2 – 8x + k =	 0	 …(2)
	 Let D1 and D2 be the discriminants of equations (1) and (2) respectively. Then,
				   D1 =	 k2 – 4 × 64 = k2 – 256 and D2 = (–8)2 – 4k = 64 – 4k
	 Both the equations will have real roots, if
				   D1 >	 0 and D2 > 0
	 ⇒		  k2 – 256 >	 0 and 64 – 4k > 0
	 ⇒		  k2 >	 256 and 64 > 4k
	 ⇒	 	 k >	 16 (Q k > 0) and k < 16
	 ⇒	 	 k =	 16
	 Hence, both the equations will have real roots, when k = 16.

Ex. 8.	 One year ago, a man was 8 times as old as his son. Now, his age is equal to the 
square of his son’s age. Find their present ages.

Sol.	 Let the son’s present age be x years.
	 Then, 	the father’s present age = x2 years.
	  	 one year ago son’s age = x – 1 years.
	 and	 father’s age	= x2 – 1 years.
	 According to the conditions given in the question,
	 One year ago father’s age = 8 times son’s age.
	 ⇒		  x2 – 1	 = 8 (x – 1)

	 ⇒		   x2 – 8x + 7	 = 0
	 ⇒		  x2 – 7x – x + 7	 = 0
 	 ⇒ 	 	 x (x – 7) – 1 (x – 7)	 = 0
	 ⇒		  (x – 7) (x – 1)	 = 0 
	 ⇒ 		  x	 = 1 or 7
	 When x = 1 ⇒ son’s age = 1 year, then father’s age = (1)2 = 1 year. Since, father’s

	 When x = 7 ⇒ son’s age = 7 years, then father’s age = (7)2 = 49 years.
Ex. 9.	 The perimeter of a right-angled triangle is five times the length of its shortest side.

	 According to the question:
	 Perimeter of the triangle = 5x.
	 Area of the triangle = 15x.

1 1
	 ⇒		  (AB)×(BC) 	 = 15x  ⇒  (AB)  x = 15x

	 ⇒		  AB	 = = 30
x

	 ⇒		  AC2	 = AB2 + BC2

	 ⇒	  	 BC	 = x = 16, AB = 30
				   AC	 = 4x – 30 = 4 (16) – 30 = 64 – 30 = 34.
		 Hence, the lengths of the three sides of the triangle are 16, 30 and 34.

MISCELLANEOUS EXAMPLES

Ex. 1.	 Solve : x2 −16 − x2 − 8x +16 = x2 − 5x + 4
Sol.	 We have,

				   x2 −16 − x2 − 8x +16 	 = x2 − 5x + 4

	 ⇒		  (x − 4)(x + 4) − (x − 4)2 	 = (x − 4)(x −1)

	 ⇒ x − 4  x + 4 − x − 4 − x −1 	 = 0

	 ⇒	 Either 	 x − 4 	 = 0
	 or		  x + 4 − x − 4 − x −1 	 = 0
	 ⇒	 	 x – 4	 = 0
 	 or		  x + 4 − x − 4 	 = x −1
	 ⇒	  	 x	 = 4	 or

SOLUTIONS FOR NCERT TEXTBOOK EXERCISES

  NCERT EXERCISE 4.1 
	 1.	 Check whether the following are quadratic equations:
	 (i)	 (x + 1)2 = 2(x – 3)			   (ii)	 x2 – 2x = (–2) (3 – x)
	 (iii)	 (x – 2) (x + 1) = (x – 1) (x + 3)	 (iv)	 (x – 3) (2x + 1) = x(x + 5)
	 (v)	 (2x – 1) (x – 3) = (x + 5) (x – 1)	   (vi)	 x2 + 3x + 1 = (x – 2)2

	 (vii)	 (x + 2)3 = 2x(x2 – 1)			  (viii)	 x3 – 4x2 – x + 1 = (x – 2)3

	Sol.	 (i)	 (x + 1)2 = 2(x – 3) ⇒ x2 + 2x + 1 = 2x – 6  ⇒  x2 + 7 = 0.
			   The equation is of the form ax2 + bx + c = 0, a ≠ 0.
			   Hence, it is a quadratic equation.
		  (ii)	 x2 – 2x = (–2) (3 – x)  ⇒ x2 – 2x = – 6 + 2x
			   ⇒	 x2 – 4x + 6	= 0.
			   The equation is of the form ax2 + bx + c = 0, a ≠ 0.
			   Hence, it is a quadratic equation.
		  (iii)		  (x – 2) (x + 1)	= (x – 1) (x + 3)
			   ⇒ 	 x2 – x – 2	= x2 + 2x – 3 ⇒ 3x – 1 = 0.
			   The equation is not of the form
				    ax2 + bx + c	= 0, a ≠ 0. N
			   Hence, it is not a quadratic equation. C
		  (iv)		  (x – 3) (2x + 1)	= x(x + 5) E
			   ⇒ 	 2x2 + x – 6x – 3	= x2 + 5x R
			   ⇒	 x2 – 10x – 3	= 0 T
			   The equation is of the form ax2 + bx + c = 0, a ≠ 0.
			   Hence, it is a quadratic equation.
		  (v)		  (2x – 1) (x – 3)	= (x + 5) (x – 1) T
			   ⇒	 2x2 – 7x + 3	= x2 + 4x – 5 E
			   ⇒	 x2 – 11x + 8	= 0. X
			   The equation is of the form ax2 + bx + c = 0, a ≠ 0. T
			   Hence, it is a quadratic equation.
		  (vi)		  x2 + 3x + 1	= (x – 2)2 B
			   ⇒	 x2 + 3x + 1	= x2 – 4x + 4 O
			   ⇒	 7x – 3	= 0 O
			   The equation is not of the form K
				    ax2 + bx + c	= 0, a ≠ 0.
			   Hence, it is not a quadratic equation.

S chand Mathematics for Class X



294    S. Chand’s MATHEMATICS FOR CLASS X

		  (vii)		  (x + 2)3	= 2x(x2 – 1)
			   ⇒	 x3 + 6x2 + 12x + 8	= 2x3 – 2x
			   ⇒	 x3 – 6x2 – 14x – 8	= 0.
			   The equation is not of the form
				    ax2 + bx + c	= 0, a ≠ 0.
			   Hence, it is not a quadratic equation.
		 (viii)		  x3 – 4x2 – x + 1	= (x – 2)3

			   ⇒	 x3 – 4x2 – x + 1	= x3 – 6x2 + 12x – 8
			   ⇒	 2x2 – 13x + 9	= 0
			   The equation is of the form ax2 + bx + c = 0, a ≠ 0.
			   Hence, it is a quadratic equation.

	 (i)	 The area of a rectangular plot is 528 m2. The length of the plot (in metres) is one

	 (i)	 Every quadratic equation has exactly one root.
	(ii)	 Every quadratic equation has at least one real root.
	(iii)	 Every quadratic equation has at least two roots.
	(iv)	 Every quadratic equation has at most two roots.
	(v)	 If the coefficient of x2 and the constant term of a quadratic equation have opposite 

signs, then the quadratic equation has real roots.
	( vi)	If the coefficient of x2 and the constant term have the same sign and if the coefficient 

of x term is zero, then the quadratic equation has no real roots.
	Sol.	 (i)	 False, because a quadratic equation has two and only two roots.
		  (ii)	 False, for example x2 + 1 = 0, has no real roots or we can say that any quadratic

		  (iii)	 False, because a quadratic equation has two and only two roots.
		  (iv)	 True, because a quadratic equation has atmost two roots.
		  (v)	 True, since in this case discriminant b2 – 4ac is alway positive. As a & c of quadratic N

equation: ax2 + bx + c are opposite in sign so (a × c) is negative so – (a × c) is positive C
so value of b2 – 4ac is  positive so roots are always real in this situation.

	 5.	 If Zeba were younger by 5 years than what she really is, then the square of her age (in 

years) would have been 11 more than five times her actual age. What is her age now?

S chand Mathematics for Class X



314    S. Chand’s MATHEMATICS FOR CLASS X

	Sol.	 Let the actual age of Zeba = x years.
		  Her age when she was 5 yr younger = (x – 5)yr
		  Now, by given condition,
		  Square of her age = 11 more than five times her actual age
			   (x – 5)2	= 5 × actual age + 11
		  ⇒	 (x – 5)2	= 5x + 11 ⇒ x2 + 25 – 10x = 5x + 11
		  ⇒	 x2 – 15x + 14	= 0
		  ⇒	 x2 – 14x – x + 14	= 0 [by spliting the middle term]
		  ⇒	 x(x – 14) – 1(x – 14)	= 0
		  ⇒	 (x – 1) (x – 14)	= 0
		  ⇒	 x	= 14
		  [here, x ≠ 1 because her age is x – 5. So, x – 5 = 1 – 5 = – 4 i.e., age cannot be in negative]

	 (iv)	 Earth completes its revolution around the sun after 12

The various numbers occurring in a pattern of numbers are called its terms.
