(d)	 Definition
Arithmetic progression (A.P.). It is a pattern of numbers in which the first term is 
given and succeeding term differs from its preceding term by a fixed number.
This fixed number is called the common difference of an Arithmetic progression.
In short, arithmetic progression is written as A.P.
Sometimes first term is denoted by T1, second term by T2 and the nth term 
(or  general  term) by Tn.
In an A.P., we usually denote the first term by ‘a’, the common difference by ‘d’ and 
the nth term by ‘tn’.
Clearly, 		  d = tn – tn–1
If the first term is a and the common difference is d then,
		  a, a + d,  a + 2d, a + 3d, ...
represents an Arithmetic progression.
This is the general form of an A.P.
To know about an A.P. the minimum information is that we should know the first term 
and common difference. If the first term is 8 and common difference is 3 then A.P. is 
		  8, 11, 14, 17, ...
Illustration. If first term is 10 and common difference is –4, then A.P. is
		  10, 6, 2, –2, –6, –10, ...
Similarly,

First term Common difference A.P.
a d a, a + d, a + 2d, a + 3d ...

12 3 12, 15, 18, 21, ...
20 –5 20, 15, 10, 5, 0, –5, ...
16 1.5 16, 17.5, 19, 20.5, 22, ...
40 –20 40, 20, 0, –20, –40, ...

We have learnt how to find an A.P., if a and d are given.
Now, we want to find out d from the given A.P., d can be obtained by subtracting any 
term from its succeeding term.
			   7, 10, 13, 16, ....; 
		    	 d = 10 – 7	 = 3
		  	 d = 13 – 10	 = 3
			   d = 16 – 13	 = 3
Let us have one more A.P. and we want to find out the common difference d.
			   1, –4, –9, –	 14, ...
			   d = – 4 – 1 =	 – 5
			   d = – 9 – (– 4) =	 – 5
			   d = – 14 – (– 9) =	 – 5

Sol.	 (i)	 2, 6, 10, 14, 18, ...
			  Here,	   6 –  2 = 4,	 10 –  6 = 4
				   14 – 10 = 4	 18 – 14 = 4
		  Here, 4 is the common difference, therefore the given pattern of numbers is 

in A.P.
	   (ii)	 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, ...
	  	 Here, 	 4 – 3 = 1	 6 – 4 = 2
				   9 – 6 = 3	 12 – 9 = 3.
		  Clearly, the differences between each pair of consecutive terms are 1, 2, 3 and 

3, which are not the same. Hence, the given pattern of numbers is not in A.P.
	 (iii)	 1, 6, 11, 16, 21, ...
			  Here, 	 6 – 1 = 5	 11 – 6 = 5
				   16 – 11 = 5	 21 – 16 = 5.
		  Clearly, 5 is the common difference, therefore the given pattern of numbers 

is in A.P.
	 (iv)	 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, ...
			  Here,	 10 – 5 = 5	 15 – 10 = 5
				   20 – 15 = 5	 30 – 20 = 10
		  Clearly, the differences between each pair of consecutive terms are 5, 5, 5 and 

10 respectively, which are not the same.
		  Thus, the given pattern of numbers is not in A.P.

Ex. 3.	 Find the common difference of the following A.P.
	 (i)	 8, 11, 14, 17, 20, ...	 (ii)	 a, a + 2d, a + 4d, a + 6d, ...
	 (iii)	 6, 1, – 4, – 9, – 14, ...	 (iv)	 2, 0.5, – 1, – 2.5, – 4, ...
Sol.	 (i)	 8, 11, 14, 17, 20, ...
			  Common difference	= Second term – First term = 11 – 8 = 3
			  Check.	 8 + 3	 = 11	 (Second term)
				   11 + 3	 = 14	 (Third term)
				   14 + 3	 = 17	 (Fourth term), etc.
			  Hence, our result is correct.
	 (ii)	 a, a + 2d, a + 4d, a + 6d, ...
			  Common difference	= Second term – First term = (a + 2d) – a = 2d
			  Check.	 a + 2d	 = a + 2d	 (Second term)
				   (a + 2d) + 2d	 = a + 4d	 (Third term)
				   (a + 4d) + 2d	 = a + 6d	 (Fourth term), etc.,
			  Hence, our result is correct.
	 (iii)	 6, 1, – 4, – 9, – 14, ...
			  Common difference =	  Second term – First term = 1 – 6 = – 5
			  Check. 	 6 + (– 5)	 = 1	 (Second term)
				   1 + (– 5)	 = – 4	 (Third term)
				   – 4 + (– 5)	 = – 9	 (Fourth term), etc.,
			  Hence, our result is correct.
	 (iv)	 2, 0.5, – 1, – 2.5, – 4, ...	
			  Common difference = Second term – First term = 0.5 – 2 = – 1.5.
			  Check.	 2 + (– 1.5)	 = 0.5	 (Second term)
				   0.5 + (– 1.5)	 = – 1	 (Third term)
				   – 1 + (– 1.5)	 = – 2.5	 (Fourth term), etc.,
			  Hence, our result is correct.

	 If	 n = 1,	 t1	 = 2 × 1 + 1 = 3

	 Here, common difference = 5 – 3 = 7 – 5 = 9 – 7 = 11 – 9 = 2.
	 Thus, 2 is the common difference and the first term = t1 = 3.
	 So, the pattern of numbers so formed is in A.P.
	 Now, if n = 12, t12 = 2 × 12 + 1 = 25.
	 \ 		  12th term	 = t12 = 25.

Ex. 8.	 If nth term of the pattern of numbers in a linear expression is n. Then, prove that 

the pattern of numbers, so formed, is an A.P. and the common difference of this 
A.P. is equal to the coefficient of n.

Sol.	 Since, given that nth term of the pattern of numbers is a linear expression.
	 \	 let it be An + B	 ⇒  tn = An + B
	 Hence, 	 t1	 = A × 1 + B = A + B
				   t2	 = A × 2 + B = 2A + B
				   t3	 = A × 3 + B = 3A + B
				   t4	 = A × 4 + B = 4A + B
				   t5	 = A × 5 + B = 5A + B.
					    ..............................................
					    ..............................................
				   tn+1	 = A (n + 1) + B
	 Here,	 t2 – t1	 = [(2A + B) – (A + B)] = A
				   t3 – t2	 = [(3A + B) – (2A + B)] = A
				   t4 – t3	 = [(4A + B) – (3A + B)] = A
				   t5 – t4	 = [(5A + B) – (4A + B)] = A
					    ..............................................
					    ..............................................
				   tn + 1 – tn	 = [A(n + 1) + B] – [An + B] = A
	 Clearly, the differences between each pair of consecutive terms are the same and 

equal to A. Hence, the pattern of numbers so formed, is an A.P.
	 and common difference = A = coefficient of n.	 Proved.

CONCEPT — 2 : GENERAL TERM OF AN A.P.
nth term of an A.P.

Let us consider an A.P. with first term ‘a’ and common difference d, then this A.P. is 
given by a, a + d, a + 2d, a + 3d, .... Clearly, in this A.P., we have
		  1st term	 =	 t1 = a + 0.d = a + (1 – 1)d
		  2nd term	 =	 t2 = a + d = a + (2 – 1)d
		  Third term	 =	 t3 = a + 2d = a + (3 – 1)d
		  Fourth term	 =	 t4 = a + 3d = a + (4 – 1)d
		 .....................................................................
	 .....................................................................
	 .....................................................................
	 .....................................................................
	 .....................................................................
	    	 nth term	 = tn = a + (n – 1) d.
In other words, from the above result we are now able to find out any term of an A.P., 
whose 1st term and common difference are known to us i.e. ‘a’ and ‘d’ respectively in 
the above case.

S chand Mathematics for Class X



324    S. Chand’s MATHEMATICS FOR CLASS X

Thus,	  nth term	= first term + (n – 1) (common difference).
		   	 tn = a + (n − 1)d

Note :	 How to select terms of an A.P. ?
	 While, solving the problems of A.P., we should select the terms in such a way, that on taking the 

sum of the terms, one unknown is eliminated automatically, as given below:
Number of terms to be selected Terms Common difference

3 a – d, a, a + d d
4 a – 3d, a – d, a + d, a + 3d 2d
5 a – 2d, a – d, a, a + d, a + 2d, d
6 a – 5d, a – 3d, a – d, a + d, a + 3d, a + 5d 2d

				   t25	 = a + (25 – 1)d = a + 24d = 2 + 24 × 3 = 74.

Ex. 12.	 Two A.Ps have the same common difference. The difference between their 100th 

terms is 100, what is the difference between their 1000 th terms?
Sol.	 Let the same common difference of two A.P. be d and their first terms be a and A 

respectively.
	 If t100 and T100 are their 100th terms, then
				   t100	 = a + (100 – 1)d
	 ⇒	 	  t100	 = a + 99d				    ...(1)
	 and 		 T100	 = A + (100 – 1)d
	 ⇒	 	 T100	 = A + 99d				    ...(2)
	 Taking difference of (1) and (2), we have
				   t100 – T100	 = (a + 99d) – (A + 99d)
	 ⇒	 	  100	 = a – A		  ...(3) [Q t100 – T100 = 100]
	 Now, 	 t1000	 = a + (1000 – 1)d                ⇒         t1000	= a + 999d
				   T1000	 = A + (1000 – 1)d                ⇒       T1000	= A + 999d
	 \		  t1000 – T1000	 = (a + 999d) – (A + 999d)
	 ⇒		   t1000 – T1000	 = a – A ⇒ t1000 – T1000 = 100			   [from (3)]
	 Hence, the difference between their 1000th terms is 100.

Ex. 23.	 If (m + 1)th term of an A.P. is twice of the (n + 1)th term, prove that (3m + 1)th 

term is twice of the (m + n + 1)th term.
Sol.	 Given, 	 tm + 1	 = 2 tn + 1
	 Let ‘a’ be the 1st term and ‘d’ the common difference of the given A.P.
	 We know that 	 tm + 1	 = a + {(m + 1) – 1} d = a + md
	 and		    tn+1	 = a + {(n + 1) – 1} d = a + nd
				   tm+1	 = 2 tn+1	 [Given]
	 ⇒	 	 a + md	 = 2 (a + nd)	
	 ⇒	 	 a	 = md – 2nd = (m – 2n)d	 ...(1)
	 Now,	  t3m + 1	 = a + {(3m + 1) – 1}d = a + 3md	 ...(2)

	 Putting the value of a from (1) in (2), we get
				   t3m + 1	 = [(m – 2n)d] + 3md = 4md – 2nd = 2d (2m – n).	 ...(4)
	 Putting the value of a from (1) in (3), we get
				    tm+n+1	 = [(m – 2n)d] + (m + n) d = 2md – nd = d (2m – n)	 ...(5)
	 From (4) and (5), we have
	 \	 	 t3m+1	 = 2d (2m – n) = 2 × tm+n+1
	 Hence, (3m + 1)th term is twice the (m + n + 1)th term.	 Proved.
Ex. 24.	 If m times the mth term of an A.P. is equal to n times its nth term, show that 

(m + n)th term of the A.P. is zero.	
Sol.	 Let ‘a’ be the 1st term and ‘d’ the common difference of the A.P., then as given,
	 m times the mth term = n times the nth term
	 ⇒		                     m.tm = n.tn, 
		 We know that, tm = a + (m – 1) d and tn = a + (n – 1) d
	 ⇒	 m.[a + (m – 1)d] = n.[a + (n – 1)d]
		 ⇒   ma + (m2 – m)d = na + (n2 – n) d
	 ⇒	 [(m2 – n2) – (m – n)]d = (n – m)a
	 ⇒	 [(m + n) (m – n) – (m – n)]d = – (m – n)a
	 ⇒	 (m – n) (m + n – 1)d = – (m – n) a 
		 ⇒  (m + n – 1)d = – a
	 ⇒	 a + {(m + n) – 1}d = 0
		 ⇒  tm+n = 0
	 Thus, the (m + n)th term of the given A.P. is zero.	 Proved.

CONCEPT — 3
(a)	 Sum of numbers

Mukul plants 1 tree in his neighbourhood park on the first birthday of his son. On 
second birthday he plants 2 trees. On third birthday he plants 3 trees and so on. How 
many trees he has planted until 20th birthday of his son. The number of trees planted 
by Mukul are :

.........................................................................................

...................................................................................

		   	                     1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + ... + 20.
To find out total number of trees planted by Mukul, we have to write each number as 
mentioned above. But it would be tedious and time consuming process. We can find 
out a short and general method for finding the sum of first n terms of an A.P.

(b)	 The sum to n th terms of an A.P.
Let us consider an A.P. containing n terms having first term equal to a, the common 
difference equal to d. Let S be the sum of n terms of this A.P. then
		  S = a + (a + d) + (a + 2d) + ... + [a + (n – 2)d] + [a + (n – 1)d]	 ...(1)
Re-writing it in reverse order, we get
	   S = [a + (n – 1)d] + [a + (n – 2)d] + [a + (n – 3)d] + ... + (a + d) + a	 ...(2)
Adding (1) and (2), termwise in pairs, we get
	 2S = [{a} + {a + (n – 1)d}] + [{a + d} + {a + (n – 2)d}]

+ [{a + (n – 2)d} + {a + d} ] + [{a + (n – 1)d}+ {a}]
	      = [2a + (n – 1)d] + [2a + (n – 1)d]+ [2a + (n – 1)d]+ ...

		  	 + [2a + (n – 1)d] + [2a + (n – 1)d]
⇒	 	 		  2S	 = n [2a + (n −1)d] 	 (since there are n terms)

n
⇒ 				    S	 = [2a + (n −1)d]

2
n

Thus, the sum of first n terms of an A.P. is Sn = [2a +(n −1)d]
2

n n
We can write this as S = [a + (a + (n − 1) d )]  Sn = [a +l]

2 2
where l is the last term of the A.P. given by l = a + (n – 1) d
Alternatively,
		   		  S	 = a + (a + d) + ⋅⋅⋅ + (l − d) + l 	 ...(3)

		   	 	 S	 = l + (l − d)+ ⋅⋅⋅ + (a + d) + a 	 ...(4)

S chand Mathematics for Class X



ARITHMETIC PROGRESSIONS    337

Adding (3) and (4) termwise in pairs, we get
	  		    2S 	= (a + l) + (a + l) + ⋅⋅⋅ + (a + l) + (a + l)
	  			   = n (a + l) 	(Since, there are n terms)

n
	  		        S 	= (a + l)

2
This form of the result is useful when the first and last terms are given and the com-
mon difference is not given.

Ex. 15.	 Prove that no matter what the real number a and b are, the pattern of numbers

Ex. 23.	 200 logs are stacked in the following manner: 20 logs in the bottom row, 19 in the

Ex. 1.	 Raghav buys a shop for ` 1,20,000. He pays half of the amount in cash and agrees 

to pay the balance in 12 annual instalments of ` 5000 each. If the rate of interest

find the total cost of the shop. (Write values)

Sol.	 Cost of shop = ` 1,20,000
	 Cash payment = ` 60,000
	 Balance = ` 1,20,000 – ` 60,000 = ` 60,000
				   First instalment	 = ` 5,000 + Interest on unpaid amount i.e. ` 60,000

		 Total payment = Half of the cost paid for the shop + payment in 12 instalments.

	 Hence total cost of the shop is ` 1,66,800.

Ex. 6.	 If the sum of n terms of an A.P. is (pn + qn2), where p and q are constants, find the 
common difference.

Sol.	 Let t1, t2, t3, ..., tn, be the given A.P., then
				   Sum	 = t1 + t2 + t3 + ... + tn = pn + qn2	 ...(1)
	 Clearly, S1 is the sum of a single term.

	 S2 is the sum of 1st two terms. S3 is the sum of 1st three terms

	 Putting  	 n	 = 1, 2, 3 in (1), we get

				   S1	 = t1 = p × (1) + q (1)2 = p + q.	 ...(2)

				   S2	 = t1 + t2 = p (2) + q (2)2 = 2p + 4q.

	 ⇒	 	  t2	 = 2p + 4q – t1	 ...(3)

	 Putting	  t1	 = p + q in (3), we get

	 ⇒	 	  t2	 = 2p + 4q – (p + q) = p + 3q.

	 Now, the common difference = t2 – t1 = p + 3q – (p + q) = 2q.

Ex. 7.	 If the sum of n terms of a progression be a quadratic expression in n, show that it 
is an A.P.

Sol.	 Let	  Sn	= an2 + bn + c, where a, b, c are constant and a ≠ 0 .
	 Then, 	 Sn–1	 = a (n – 1)2 + b(n – 1) + c = a (n2 – 2n + 1) + b (n – 1) + c.
	 As we know that tn = Sn – Sn–1.
	 ⇒		  tn	 = (an2 + bn + c) – (an2 – 2an + a + bn – b + c).
					    = 2an – a + b = 2an + (b – a).
	 ⇒	 	   tn	 = 2an + (b – a).	 ...(1)
	 Clearly, equation (1) is a linear expression in n and we know that if nth term of a 

progression is a linear expression in n, then it is an A.P.
	 Therefore, the given expression is an A.P.	 Proved.

Ex. 12.	 If a, b, c are in A.P., prove that the following are also in A.P.
	 (i)	 b + c, c + a, a + b		                        (ii) a2 (b + c), b2 (c + a), c2 (a + b)

1 1 1 1 1 1
	 (iii)	 , ,            (iv) , ,

Sol.	 (i)  b + c, c + a, a + b will be in A.P.
			         if  	 (c + a) – (b + c)	 = (a + b) – (c + a)
			  ⇒   if	  a – b	 = b – c.
			  ⇒   if	  2b	 = a + c
			  ⇒  if a, b, c are in A.P.
			  Thus, a, b, c are in A.P. ⇒ (b + c), (c + a), (a + b) are in A.P.	 Proved.
	  (ii)	 a2 (b + c), b2 (c + a), c2 (a + b) will be in A.P.
			  if 	b2 (c + a) – a2 (b + c) = c2 (a + b) – b2 (c + a).
			  ⇒ if c (b2 – a2) + ab (b – a) = a (c2 – b2) + bc (c – b).
			  ⇒ if c(b – a) (b + a) + ab (b – a) = a (c – b) (c + b) + bc (c – b).
			  ⇒ if (b – a) [ab + bc + ca] = (c – b) [ab + bc + ca].
			  ⇒ if	 b – a	 = c – b  ⇒   2b = a + c
			  ⇒	 if a, b, c are in A.P.
			  Thus, a, b, c are in A.P. ⇒ a2(b + c), b2 (c + a), c2(a + b) are in A.P.	 Proved.

	 1.	 Fill in the blanks in the following table, given that a is the first term, d the common

a d n an

	Sol.	 (i)	 Here, a = 7, d = 3 and n = 8, Hence an = a + (n – 1)d = 7 + (8 – 1) × 3 = 28

C 		  (ii)	 Here; a = – 18, n = 10 and an = 0, so by using an =  a + (n – 1)d, we get: 0 = – 18 + 
E (10 – 1)d ⇒ d = 2

	 4.	 Two APs have the same common difference. The first term of one AP is 2 and that of the 
other is 7. The difference between their 10th terms is the same as the difference between 
their 21st terms, which is the same as the difference between any two corresponding 
terms. Why?

	Sol.	 Let common differences of both APs = d
		  As first term of first A.P. is 2 and of second A.P. is 7
		  So two APs are: 
		  (i) 2, 2 + d, 2 + 2d, 2 + 3d, ...	 (ii)	7, 7 + d, 7 + 2d, 7 + 3d, ...
		  Now difference between their 10th terms = 2 + 9d – (7 + 9d) = – 5
		  Difference between their 21st terms = 2 + 20d – (7 + 20d) = – 5
		  Let nth term of first AP is = 2 + (n – 1)d
		  and nth term of second AP = 7 + (n – 1)d
		  Now the difference between their nth term
				   = {2 + (n – 1)d} – {7 + (n – 1)d}
				   = 2 + (n – 1)d – 7 – (n – 1)d
				   = – 5
		  Hence difference between any two corresponding terms is always same and equal to 

difference between their first terms.

6 Similar Triangles

  TOPICS

CONCEPT – 1 : SIMILARITY IN DIFFERENT POLYGONS
(a)	 Similar Figures

Geometric figures, having the same shape are known as similar figures.
Two congruent figures are always similar, but two similar figures may or may not be 

congruent.
To grasp the concept of similarity let us have two photographs of a person having 

different sizes made from the same negative, the corresponding line segments of the 
two photographs are observed to be proportional and the angle between any pair of 
corresponding line segments is equal. This is due to the fact that whenever a photographer 
wants to make photographs of different sizes, then he performs his requirement either by 
reducing or by enlarging the size to the desired scale [1.5 times (bigger) or 0.8 times (smaller), 
etc.]. Hence, we observe that all such photographs are similar to each other.

The reduced and enlarged photographs of a person made from the same negative 
are similar.

Similar Photographs

Similar line segments

403



404    S. Chand’s MATHEMATICS FOR CLASS X

Similar triangles

Circles are always similar

Similar Squares

Thus, we conclude that if we have two figures and out of these two one can be obtained 
either by shrinking or by Stretching the other, as in the above examples, then the two figures 
are similar. There is one to one correspondence between the parts of two similar figures.

Two polygons are said to be similar to each other, if
	 (i)	 their corresponding angles are equal and
	(ii)	 the lengths of their corresponding sides are proportional.
Two similar polygons ABCDEF and PQRSTU, in symbolic form are written as polygon 

ABCDEF ~ polygon PQRSTU, where the symbol ‘~’ stands for “is similar to.”

All regular polygons of the same number of sides such as equilateral triangles, squares, etc., 
are similar. In particular, all circles are also similar.

Note:	 Proportion : The equality of two ratios is called proportion. Four quantities a, b, c, d are 
said to be in proportion.

a c
	 if a : b = c : d or = .

b d

B A E D

The above figures are not similar because
	 (i)	 The corresponding angles in some figures are not equal.
	(ii)	 The corresponding sides are not proportional in some figures.
	(iii)	 In some figures neither angles are equal nor sides are proportional.

Note:	 In the case of two similar polygons, the two conditions given in the definition are inde-
pendent of each other. It means, if the corresponding angles of two polygons are equal, 
but lengths of their corresponding sides are not proportional or vice-versa, the polygons 
will not be similar.

We keep a table below a lighted bulb fitted in the ceiling. We place a quadrilateral or 

polygon cut from a cardboard between the lighted 
bulb and the table and it should be parallel to the 
table.

Then a shadow of ABCD is cast on the table. 
Marking the outlines of this shadow we find 
quadrilateral A′B′C′D′. Quadrilateral A′B′C′D′ is an 
enlargement (or magnification) of the quadrilateral 
ABCD. Enlargement is due to the property of light 
that light propogates in a straight line. A′, B′, C′ 
and D′ lie on the extended lines OA, OB, OC, 
OD respectively. So, the quadrilateral A′B′C′D′ is 
similar to quadrilateral ABCD. On measuring the 
angles and the sides of the quadrilateral ABCD and 
A′B′C′D′. We verify that

	 (i)	 ∠A = ∠A′, ∠B = ∠B′, ∠C = ∠C′, and 
∠D = ∠D′.

AB BC CD DA
	(ii)	 = = =

A′B′ B′C′ C′D′ D′A′
Now, it is verified that :
Two polygons of the same number of sides are similar, if
	 (i)	 all the corresponding angles are equal and
	(ii)	 all the corresponding sides are in the same ratio (or proportional).
Hence, quadrilateral ABCD and A′B′C′D′ are similar.

(e)	 Square and Rectangle
A rectangle ABCD and a square PQRS are of equal corresponding angles. But their 

corresponding sides are not in the same ratio.

SIMILAR TRIANGLES    407

Hence, the rectangle ABCD and square PQRS are not similar.
(f )	 Square and Rhombus

Corresponding sides of square ABCD and rhombus PQRS are in the same ratio, but 
their corresponding angles are not equal. So, they are not similar.

In case of polygon the following three conditions are necessary to make them similar.
	 (i)	 Number of sides in one polygon equal to number of sides in other polygon.
	(ii)	 The corresponding angles are equal.
	(iii)	 Length of their corresponding sides are proportional.

CONCEPT – 3 : CRITERION FOR SIMILARITY OF TRIANGLES
We have already stated that two triangles are similar if
	 (i)	 their corresponding angles are equal.
	(ii)	 their corresponding sides are in the same ratio (proportional).
So, in DABC and DDEF
If (i)	 ∠A =	 ∠D, ∠B = ∠E, ∠C = ∠F

AB BC CA
and (ii)	  =	 =

DE EF FD
then two triangles DABC and DDEF are similar.
i.e.,	 DABC ~	 DDEF.

S chand Mathematics for Class X



422    S. Chand’s MATHEMATICS FOR CLASS X

In case of congruency or similarity of two triangles we should use correct correspondence 
of their vertices for example

	D ABC ~	DDEF
But not in the following manner.
	D ABC ~	DEDF
	D ABC ~	DEFD
	D ABC ~	DFED
	D ABC ~	DFDE
We should not ignore the correct correspondence of the vertices.

Theorem 3. (AAA Similarity) If in two triangles, corresponding angles are equal, 
then their corresponding sides are in the same ratio (or proportional) and hence the two 
triangles are similar.

Given. In two ∆s ABC and DEF
                         ∠A = ∠D, ∠B = ∠E and ∠C = ∠F.
To prove.  DABC ~ DDEF
Proof. Case I. When AB = DE
	 ∠A 	= ∠D
	 ∠B 	= ∠E, ∠C = ∠F and AB = DE
	 DABC 	≅ DDEF               (By ASA congruence theorem)
⇒	 AB 	= DE, BC = EF and AC = DF

AB BC AC
⇒	 	 = =

DE EF DF
Hence,	 DABC	 ~ DDEF
Case II. When AB < DE
	Take a point P on line DE and Q on the line DF such that AB = DP and AC = DQ, join

Theorem 4. (SSS similarity) If in two triangles, sides of one triangle are proportional 
to (i.e. in the same ratio of) the sides of the other triangle, then their corresponding 
angles are equal and hence the two triangles are similar.

CONCEPT – 5 : AREAS OF SIMILAR TRIANGLES
The ratio of the areas of two similar triangles has relation with the ratio of the corresponding 

sides. The ratio of the areas of two similar triangles is the square of the ratio of their corresponding 
sides.

CONCEPT – 6 : PYTHAGORAS THEOREM OR  
BAUDHAYAN THEOREM

Statement. In any right angled triangle square of length of hypotenuse (Longest side) 
is equal to sum of squares of lengths of other two sides (i.e., Base and Perpendicular)
Given. DABC, right angled at B.
To Prove.	 AC2 =	 AB2 + BC2

Proof. In DABC and DADB

Statement. In any triangle if square of length of longest side is equal to sum of squares 

of lengths of other two sides then angle opposite to longest side is 90°.

	 PR2 =	 AB2 + BC2	 ...(2)

Ex. 5.	 Nazima is fly fishing in a stream. The tip of her fishing rod is 1.8 m above the 

surface of the water and the fly at the end of the string rests on the water 3.6 m 
away and 2.4 m from a point directly under the tip of the rod. Assuming that her 
string (from the tip of her rod to the fly) is taut, how much string does she have 
out (see fig.)? If she pulls in the string at the rate of 5 cm per second, what will be 
the horizontal distance of the fly from her after 12 seconds ?

                                  (NCERT Textbook)
Sol.	 Let O be the position of Nazima at the time of fishing.

	 12.	 Is it true to say that, if in two triangles, an angle of one triangle is equal to an angle of 
another triangle and two sides of one triangle are proportional to the two sides of the 

P Q
other triangle, then the triangles are similar? Give reason for your answer.

	Sol.	 False. Because according to SAS similarity criterion, if one angle of a triangle is equal 
to one angle of the other triangle and the sides including these angles are proportional, 
then the two triangles are similar.

		  Here, one angle and two sides of two triangles are equal but these sides not including 
equal angle, so given statement is not correct.

INTRODUCTION
We have already done introductory studies of co-ordinate geometry in class IX. Now, 
in class X we will iterate it and go in detail.
We will learn geometrical representation of quadratic polynomials, distance formula, 
section formula and area of a triangle.

CO-ORDINATE GEOMETRY
It is a branch of geometry which sets up a definite correspondence between the position 
of a point in a plane and a pair of algebraic numbers, called co-ordinates.
Co-ordinate geometry has been developed as an algebraic tool for studying the 
geometry of objects. It helps us to study geometry using algebra, and understand 
algebra with the help of geometry.

(a)	 Cartesian Co-ordinates (Rectangular co-ordinates)
In Cartesian co-ordinates the position of a point P is 
determined by knowing the distances from two 
perpendicular lines passing through the fixed point. 
Let O be the fixed point called the origin and XOX′  
and YOY′ , the two perpendicular lines through O, 
called Cartesian or Rectangular co-ordinates axes.
Draw PM and PN perpendiculars on OX and OY 
respectively. OM (or NP) is called the x co-ordinate or 
abscissa of the point P. ON (or MP) is called the y co-
ordinate or the ordinate of the point P.
The abscissa and ordinate of a point taken together is known as co-ordinates of a point.
If OM = x, ON = y, the co-ordinates of the point P are (x, y). These co-ordinates are 
called the Cartesian co-ordinates of P.
Notation. OM and MP are denoted by x and y respectively.

521



522    S. Chand’s MATHEMATICS FOR CLASS X

(b)	 Axes of co-ordinates
In the figure OX and OY are called as x-axis and y-axis respectively and both together 
are known as axes of co-ordinates.

(c)	 Origin
Origin is point O of intersection of the axes of co-ordinates.

(d)	 Abscissa
The distance of the point P from y-axis is called its abscissa. In the figure OM is the 

abscissa.

(e )	 Ordinate
The distance of the point P from x-axis is called its ordinate. ON is the ordinate in the 

figure.

(f)	 Quadrant
1

A quadrant is  part of a plane divided by co-ordinate axes.
4

	 (i)	 XOY is called the first quadrant.
	 (ii)	 YOX′  the second.
	 (iii)	 X′OY′  the third.
	 (iv)	 Y′OX  the fourth as marked in the figure.

(g)	 Rules for Signs of Co-ordinates
	 (i)	 In the first quadrant, both co-ordinates i.e., abscissa 

and ordinate of a point are positive.
	 (ii)	 In the second quadrant, for a point, abscissa is 

negative and ordinate is positive.
	 (iii)	 In the third quadrant, for a point, both abscissa and 

ordinate are negative.
	 (iv)	 In the fourth quadrant, for a point, the abscissa is 

positive and the ordinate is negative.

	 Quadrant	 x-co-ordinate	 y-co-ordinate	  Co-ordinates
	 First quadrant	 +	 +	 (+, +)
	 Second quadrant	 –	 +	 (–, +)
	 Third quadrant	 –	 –	 (–, –)
	 Fourth quadrant 	 +	 –	 (+, –)

CONCEPT – 2 : SIGNIFICANCE OF SECTION FORMULA
Karina, resident of Lucknow got admission in Delhi School. She knows the location 
of railway station and the school. She wants to know the location of a post office. 
Post office, railway station and school are situated in a straight line. The post office is 
between the railway station and the school. Distance between the post office and the 
school is twice the distance between the railway station and the post office.

AB 2
Let A, B, C represent school, post office and railway station. Let =

BC 1

We will solve her problem by following Ratio Formula.

(a)	 Ratio formula for internal Division (section formula)
A point C divides the straight line joining two points A (x1, y1) and B (x2, y2) internally 
in the ratio m1 : m2; to find the co-ordinates of C.
Let the co-ordinates of C be (x, y). Draw perpendiculars AL, BM and CN on the x-axis 

S chand Mathematics for Class X



530    S. Chand’s MATHEMATICS FOR CLASS X

from A, B and C respectively. Draw AP and CQ perpendiculars from A and C on CN 
and BM respectively.
		  AP	 = LN = ON – OL = x – x1,
		 CQ	 = NM = OM – ON = x2 – x,
		 CP	 = NC – NP = NC – LA = y – y1 and
		 BQ	 = MB – MQ = MB – NC = y2 – y.
Then, from the similar ∆s ACP and CBQ, we have

AP AC x − x m

CQ CB x2 − x m2

	⇒	 (m1 + m2)x	 = m1 x2 + m2 x1

m
		 x	 = 1x2 +m2x1

m1 +m2

Again, from the similar ∆s ACP and CBQ, we have
CP AC y − y m

		  	 = or 1 = 1
BQ CB y2 − y m2

⇒ 	 m2 (y – y1)	 = m1 (y2 – y),
⇒ 	 (m1 + m2) y	 = m1 y2 + m2 y1

m

m1 +m2

Hence, the co-ordinates of point C which divides the straight line joining two points 
(x1, y1) and (x2, y2) internally in the ratio m1 : m2 are:

The co-ordinates of a point which divides the straight line joining two points (x1, y1)

Sign of Area. If three points A, B, C are taken in the anticlockwise sense, then the area 
calculated of the triangle ABC will be positive, while if the points are taken in clockwise 
sense, then the area calculated will be negative.

In case the area calculated is negative we shall consider it positive.

(b)	 Condition of Collinearity of Three points
		  x1(y2 – y3) + x2(y3 – y1) + x3(y1 – y2) = 0

which can also be written in the form:

Ex 2.	 Find a relation between x and y, if the points (x, y), (1, 2) and (7, 0) are collinear.

[NCERT Textbook]
Sol.	 The points A (x, y), B (1, 2) and C (7, 0) will be collinear, if 
	                   x (2 – 0) + 1(0 – y) + 7(y – 2)	= 0
	 i.e., 		  2x – y + 7y – 14	 = 0
	 or		   2x + 6y – 14	 = 0
	 or		  x + 3y – 7	 = 0
	 which is the required relation between x and y.

Ex. 4.	 The two opposite vertices of a square are (– 1, 2) and (3, 2). Find the coordinates 

of the other two vertices.		                                    [NCERT Textbook]
Sol.	 Let ABCD be a square and let A (– 1, 2) and C (3, 2) be the given opposite vertices.

	 So,	  (x + 1)2 + (y – 2)2	 = (x – 3)2 + (y – 2)2

	 or	 2x + 1	 = – 6x + 9

8 Introduction to 
Trigonometry

TOPICS

1.	 Introduction	 2.	Trigonometic Ratios
3.	 Trigonometric Ratios of some specific angles

INTRODUCTION
In previous classes we have studied 

about right triangles and their properties. As 
we know, one angle in right triangle is right 
angle and the side opposite to the right angle 
is known as hypotenuse.

Sometimes we observe imaginary right 
triangle in nature. For instance,
	 1.	 During my visit to Mumbai, I went 

to Marine Drive where I saw the top 
of coconut tree. I imagined a right 
triangle formed by tree, base line and line of sight.

	 2.	 In Paris Anil saw the Eifel tower. He imagined a right triangle, formed by Eifel 
tower base line and line of sight. He was thinking how high tower is ?

581



582    S. Chand’s MATHEMATICS FOR CLASS X

	 3.	 In Haridwar, Aakriti was staying on the fourth floor of a hotel located on the 
bank of Ganges river. From the balcony of the room she is looking down at a boat 
lying on the other bank of the river. A right triangle is imagined to be formed by 
building, width of the river and the line of sight. She was thinking how to measure 
the width of the river.

The height of the coconut tree, height of Eifel Tower and width of the Ganges river, 
can be found with the help of trigonometry.
Trigonometry is a word derived from three Greek words
	 Tri – Three
	 gonia – Angle	 i.e., triangle measure.
	 metron – Measure
Thus trigonometry literally means measurement of triangle. It is at present considered 
to be that branch of mathematics which deals with the measurement of angles and the 
problems related with angles. In this way trigonometry is the study of relationship 
between sides and angles of a triangle.

CONCEPT – 1 : TRIGONOMETRIC RATIOS
Now, we will learn the ratio of sides of a right triangle called trigonometric ratios of angles.
Till now we have seen some imaginary right triangles in above examples.

(c)	 Value of Trigonometric Ratios

The value of trigonometric ratio remains the same for the C
same angle of different right triangles.

the hypotenuse AC of right triangle DABC and draw

CONCEPT – 2 : TRIGONOMETRIC RATIOS OF SOME SPECIFIC ANGLES
(i) Trigonometric ratios of 0°

∠A is made smaller and smaller in the right  till it becomes zero. As ∠A gets smaller 
and smaller the length of the side BC decreases. The point C gets closer to the point B and 
finally when ∠A becomes very close to 0°, AC becomes almost the same as AB, and BC gets 
very close to 0.

CONCEPT – 3 : TRIGONOMETRIC RATIOS OF COMPLEMENTARY ANGLES
Theorem : If q is an acute angle, then

	 (i)	sin(90° – q) = cos q	 (ii)	cos(90° – q) = sin q	
	 (iii)	tan(90° – q) = cot q	 (iv)	cot(90° – q) = tan q	
	 (v)	sec(90° – q) = cosec q	 (vi)	cosec(90° – q) = sec q

Construction. Draw a right angled triangle ABC right angled at B.
Proof.
Let ∠A = q, then ∠C = 90° – q C

Ex. 5.	 Find the value of each of the following without using trigonometric tables :
	 	(i)	 tan (55° – q) – cot(35° + q)       (ii) cosec (65° + q) – sec (25° – q)	
Sol.		 (i)	 tan(55° – q) – cot(35° + q) = tan(55° – q) – cot (90° – 55° + q)
			  = 	tan(55° – q) – cot[90° – (55° – q)] = tan(55° – q) – tan(55° – q) = 0	
		 (ii)	 cosec (65° + q) – sec (25° – q) = cosec (90° – 25° + q) – sec (25° – q)
			  = 	cosec [90° – (25° – q)] – sec (25 – q) = sec (25° – q) – sec (25° – q) = 0 	
Ex. 6.	 Evaluate: cosec (65° + q) – sec (25° – q) – tan(55° – q) + cot(35° + q) 	
Sol.	 cosec(65° + q) – sec (25° – q) – tan(55° – q) + cot (35° + q)
			  =	cosec(90° – 25° + q) – sec(25° – q) – tan(90° – 35° – q) + cot(35° + q)
			  = 	cosec[90° – (25° – q)] – sec (25° – q) – tan [90° – (35° + q)] + cot (35° + q)
			  = 	sec(25° – q) – sec(25° – q) – cot(35° + q) + cot(35° + q) = 0

Ex. 8.	 If tan 2A = cot (A – 18°), where 2A is an acute angle, find the value of A.

[NCERT Textbook]
Sol.	 We have,	           tan 2A =	 cot (A – 18°)	 ... (1)
	 ⇒		  cot (90° – 2A) =	 cot (A – 18°)	 [Q cot (90° – 2A) = tan 2A]
	 ⇒	    	     90° – 2A =	 A – 18°
	 ⇒	                  	 3A =	 108°	 [Q 90° – 2A and A – 18° both are acute angles]
	 ⇒		  ∠A =	 36°	
Ex. 9.	 If tan A = cot B, prove that A + B = 90°.	
Sol.	 We have,	 tan A =	 cot B
	 ⇒		  tan A =	 tan(90° – B)	 [Q tan (90° – B) = cot B]
	 ⇒		  A =	 90° – B
	 ⇒	           	 A + B =	 90°	 Proved.
Ex. 10.	 If sec 4A = cosec (A – 20°), where 4A is an acute angle, find the value of A.	

[NCERT Textbook]
Sol.	 We have,	 sec 4A =	 cosec (A – 20°)
	 ⇒		  cosec (90° – 4A) =	 cosec (A – 20°)         	 [Q cosec (90° – q) = sec q]
	 ⇒	           	 90° – 4A =	 A – 20°   ⇒   5A = 90° + 20°
	 ⇒		  5A =	 110°        ⇒   ∠A = 22°

9 Heights & Distances

TOPICS
	 1.	 Line of sight	                      2. Angle of elevation                3. Angle of depression
	 4.	 Use of angles 30°, 45° and 60° for solving problems on heights and distances.

INTRODUCTION
Ancient astronomers have used trigonometry to calculate the distance from earth 
to the stars. Maps are constructed with the help of the knowledge of trigonometry. 
Trigonometry is used in everyday life around us.
Sometimes it may not be easily possible to measure with a measuring tape the height 
of a big tree, apartment, tower, the width of a river and the distance between a ship 
and the light-house. We can determine these with the knowledge of trigonometry.

Distance

CO
	 	Let us define some basic terms. PT – 1

659



660    S. Chand’s MATHEMATICS FOR CLASS X

CONCEPT – 1 

(a)	 LINE OF SIGHT (LINE OF VISION)
The line of sight is the imaginary line drawn from 

the eye of the observer to the top of a minar, when a 
person is looking at the top of the minar.

(b)	 ANGLE OF ELEVATION
Let P be the position of an object above 

the horizontal line OX, where O is the position 
of the eye of an observer looking upward at 
the object. Then,∠XOP  is called the angle of 
elevation.

(c)	 ANGLE OF DEPRESSION
Let P be the position of an object below the 

horizontal line OX, where O is the position of the eye of 
an observer looking downward at the object, then ∠XOP  
is called the angle of depression.

(d)	 WORKING RULE TO FIND THE HEIGHT OF THE MINAR
We should know the following:
Step 1. Horizontal distance AB between the eye and the 
foot of the minar.
Step 2. Angle of elevation∠BAC  of the top of the minar.

Ex. 35.	 The angle of elevation of the top a tower from two points at a distance of 4 m and 9 m 

from the base of the tower and in the same straight line with it are complementary. 
Prove that the height of the tower is 6 m.	 [NCERT Textbook]

Sol.	 Let AB be the tower. Let C and D be the two points at distance 9 m and 4 m 
respectively from the base of the tower. Then, AC = 9 m and AD = 4 m.

	 Let ∠ ACB = θ then ∠ ADB = 90° – θ.	 [Q Angles are complementry]
	 Let h metres be the height of the tower AB.

10 Circles

 TOPICS
1.	 Introduction to circles	 2.	 Tangent to circle
3.	 Circles and common tangents	 4.	 Secant to a circle
5.	 Properties of tangents, secant and intersecting lines

CONCEPT – 1 

(a)   INTRODUCTION
We have already studied circles and various terms related to circles in the previous 
class. Now you are able to understand some other facts as well as like tangents to a 
circle and their properties.
Consider a circle and a line AB. There are three cases regarding the position of the line 
with respect to the circle as shown in the following figures.

Case I.	 The line AB and the circle have no common point.
	 The line AB does not intersect the circle and it is outside the circle.
	 AB is called a non-intersecting line with respect to the circle.
Case II.	 There are two common points C and D between the line AB and the circle. 

The line AB intersects the circle in two distinct points C and D. Then, the line 
AB is called a secant of the circle.

Definition. A line, which intersects a circle in two distinct points, is called a secant 
of the circle.

707



708    S. Chand’s MATHEMATICS FOR CLASS X

Case III. Line AB intersects the circle in two coincident points or in exactly one point 
C. Here, line AB is said to touch the circle at a point C, or line AB is a tangent 
to the circle at the point C. The point C is called the point of contact of line 
AB with the circle. This point is common to the tangent and the circle.

Definition. A line meeting a circle only in one point is called a tangent to the circle.
Point of contact. The point, at which the 
line touches the circle (at one point), is 
called the point of contact. The point of 
contact is the only point, which is common 
to the tangent and the circle.
Illustration I
If we look at the wheels of a moving cycle, 
the wheel moves on the ground along a 
line, which is tangent to the wheel.
Illustration II
This concept can also be illustrated by the following example.

Railway Track

Moving wheel

You must have seen train several times. Have you ever noticed about the position of 
these railway tracks and the wheels of the train? If yes, you might have seen that the 
railway track is a straight path and the wheels of the train move on these tracks. The 
wheels are always in contact with the track. Hence, we say that the track is tangent 
to the wheels of the train.

(b)   TANGENT TO A CIRCLE
By performing the following activities we can understand the existence of a tangent 
to a circle at a point.

ACTIVITY – 1
We take a wire and bend it in the circular form. We also take another straight wire AB 
and attach it to the circular wire at P.
Put the circular wire with the attached straight wire AB on the table. We rotate the 
wire AB 	about the point P, then the points Q1, Q2, Q3 moves towards P and the point 
Q comes nearer and nearer to the point P. A stage comes when the point Q coincides 
with the point P. The line AB will touch the circle at P. In this way, the wire AB becomes 
the tangent to the circle at P.

S chand Mathematics for Class X



CIRCLES    709

On rotating further we observe that in all other positions of AB, it will intersect the 
circle at P and on other points, say R1 or R2 or R3.
Thus, there is only one tangent at a point of the circle.

ACTIVITY – 2
We draw a circle and a secant AB of the circle on a paper. We also draw few lines 
parallel to the secant AB on both sides of it. Here we find that the length of the chords 
cut by the lines on upper side increases and then gradually decreases.
On the other side the length of chords will gradually 

decrease i.e. the two points of intersection of the line AB and 
the circle are coming closer and closer. On one side the length 
becomes zero. At this point the line becomes a tangent on the 
other side of the secant AB the length also becomes zero. Here 
again there is another tangent at this point. In this way, two 
tangents are formed. Thus we find that there cannot be more 
than two tangents parallel to the given secant.

Both activities confirm the belief that a tangent is the secant where both of the end 
points of the corresponding chord coincide.

The common point of the tangent and the circle is called the point of contact and the 
tangent is said to touch the circle at the common point.

(c)   PROPERTIES OF TANGENTS
	 (i)	 The tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to 

the radius through the point of contact.
		  Tangent ⊥ Radius, i.e., OP ⊥ PT.

	 (ii)	 The lengths of tangents drawn from an external 
point to a circle are equal.

		  i.e., 		  PA = PB

Theorem 1. The tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through 
the point of contact.

Given. A circle C (O, r) and a tangent AB at a point P.
To prove. 	 OP	⊥ AB

S chand Mathematics for Class X



710    S. Chand’s MATHEMATICS FOR CLASS X

Construction. Take any point Q, other than P, on the tangent AB. Join OQ.
Proof. Since, Q is a point on the tangent AB, other than the point of contact P, so Q 
will be outside the circle.
Let OQ intersect the circle at R.
		  OQ	= OR + RQ
⇒		  OQ	> OR
⇒		  OQ	> OP       (OR = OP = radius)
\		  OP	< OQ
Thus, OP is shorter than any other segment joining O to any point of AB.
But, among all line segments, joining the point O to a point on AB, the shortest one 
is the perpendicular from O on AB.
Hence,	    OP	⊥ AB	

Q.E.D.
Converse of Theorem 1. A line drawn through the end of a radius and perpendicular 
to it, is a tangent to the circle.
Given. A radius OP of a circle C (O, r) and a line APB, 

perpendicular to OP.
To prove. AB is a tangent to the circle at the point P.
Proof. Consider a point Q on the line different from P.
Since, 	    OP	⊥ AB
OP is the shortest distance between the centre O and the all other points (except P) 

on the line.
⇒		  OP	< OQ
⇒		  OQ	> OP
⇒ Q lies outside the circle.
⇒ All the points, except P, lie outside the circle. It means that AB meets the circle only 

at the point P. Hence, AB is a tangent to the circle at P.                                                  Q.E.D.

Note : The line containing the radius through the point of contact is also sometimes called  
                “normal” to the circle at the point.

CONCEPT – 2 
Case 1. A point inside the circle:
We draw a circle on a paper and mark a point P inside the 

circle. From this point we try to draw tangent to the circle but the 
lines through this point P intersect the circles at two points and we 
did not find a single tangent.

Case 2. A point on the circle:
Now we take point P on the circle and we try to draw a tangent 

through this point. We get only one tangent PT through the point P.
Case 3. A point outside the circle:
Now we take the point P outside the circle from this point. 

We try to draw the tangents to the given circle. Here we get two 
tangents PT and PQ from the point P to the given circle.

(a)	 NUMBER OF TANGENTS TO A CIRCLE FROM A POINT
The number of tangents drawn from a point to a circle depends upon the position of 

the point with respect to the circle.

	 (i)	 If a point P lies inside the circle, any line passing through the point will intersect 
the circle at two points and therefore, cannot be a tangent.

	 (ii)	 In the figure (ii) point P lies on a circle, only one tangent can be drawn to the 
circle through the point of contact P.

	 (iii)	 If point P lies outside the circle, two tangents can be drawn to the circle from 
the point P as in figure (iii).

S chand Mathematics for Class X



CIRCLES    713

(b)	 LENGTH OF THE TANGENT
The length of a tangent is the length of the segment of the 
tangent between the point and the given point of contact on 
the circle.
In the figure, length of tangent is PT.
Theorem 2. The lengths of tangents drawn from an external 
point to a circle, are equal.
Given. AP and AQ are two tangents, from A to a circle C (O, r)
To prove.	                                    AP = AQ
Construction. Join OP, OQ and OA.
Proof. In DOPA and DOQA
		  OP	= OQ	 (Radii of the same circle)
		  ∠OPA	= ∠OQA	 (OP ⊥ AP and OQ ⊥ AQ)
		  OA	= OA 	 (Common)
	 \   	 ∆OPA	@ ∆OQA	 ...(1) (R.H.S. Theorem of congruence)
		  AP	= AQ	  (C.P.C.T.) Q.E.D.
Corollary. From (1), we have
		   ∠OAP	= ∠OAQ	 (C.P.C.T)

1
⇒	  	 ∠OAP	= ∠PAQ

2
i.e., OA is bisector of ∠PAQ .

	 ⇒ 	 Radius of the circle	= 5 cm

Ex. 12.	 Prove that the tangents drawn at the ends of a diameter of a circle are parallel.	
						     [NCERT Textbook]

	 Proof. AB ⊥ PQ  and AB ⊥ RS

	 ⇒		  ∠PAB 	 = 90°
	 and		  ∠ABS 	 = 90°
	 ⇒		   ∠PAB 	 = ∠ABS

	 ⇒ 		  PQ	 ||RS  [ ∠PAB and ∠ABS
Q  are alternate angles] Q.E.D.

Ex. 15.	 In fig. XY and X′Y′are two parallel tangents to a circle with centre O and another 

tangent AB with point of contact C intersecting XY at A and X′Y′ at B. Prove that 
∠AOB = 90°.			   [NCERT Textbook]

tangent.

	 To prove.
				   ∠AOB	 = 90°
	 Proof. We know that
	 AO is bisector of ∠XAC

2

1

	 ⇒		  ∠OBC	 = ∠CBX′       	    ...(2)
2

	 XY and X′Y′ are parallel lines, AB is transversal.
	 ⇒ 		  ∠XAC + ∠CBX′ 	 = 180°
	 (Sum of interior angles of the same side of the transversal = 180°)

1 1
 	 ⇒		  ∠XAC + ∠CBX′ 	 = 90°

2 2
	 ⇒		   ∠OAC + ∠OBC 	 = 90°	 [From (1) and (2)]
	 ⇒		   ∠OAB + ∠OBA 	 = 90°	 ...(3)
 	 Now 	∠AOB + (∠OAB + ∠OBA)  = 180°	 [Sum of angles of D AOB = 180° ]
	 ⇒		  ∠AOB + 90° 	 = 180°
	 ⇒		   ∠AOB 	 = 180° − 90° = 90° 	 [From (3)]
	 Thus,                          ∠AOB = 90° 	 Proved.

Ex. 17.	 Prove that the parallelogram circumscribing a circle is a rhombus. [NCERT Textbook]
Sol.	 Given. Sides AB, BC, CD and DA of a ||  gm ABCD touch a circle at P, Q, R and S 

respectively.
	 To prove. ||gm ABCD is a rhombus.
	 Proof.	 AP	 = AS	  ...(1)
				   BP	 = BQ	  ...(2)
				   CR	 = CQ	 ...(3)

Tangents drawn from an external
				   DR	 = DS	 ...(4)  point to a circle are equal 

 
	 Adding (1), (2), (3) and (4), we get
	    		  AP + BP + CR + DR	 = AS + BQ + CQ + DS
	 ⇒     (AP + BP) + (CR + DR)	= (AS + DS) + (BQ + CQ)
	 ⇒	  	      AB + CD	 = AD + BC
	 ⇒	 	 AB + AB	 = AD + AD	 [In a ||gm ABCD, opp. sides are equal]
	 ⇒	  	    2 AB	 = 2AD or AB = AD	 ...(5)
	 But,		  AB	 = CD and AD = BC	 ...(6) [Opposite sides of a ||gm].
	 \		  AB	 = BC = CD = DA	 [From (5) and (6)]
	 Hence, ||gm ABCD is a rhombus.	 Q.E.D.
Ex. 18.	 A triangle ABC is drawn to circumscribe a circle of 

radius 4 cm such that the segments BD and DC into 
which BC is divided by the point of contact D are of 
lengths 8 cm and 6 cm respectively (See figure). Find 
the sides AB and AC.	                      [NCERT Textbook]

Sol.	 Let the ∆ ABC be drawn to circumscribe a circle with 
centre O and radius 4 cm.

	 i.e., the circle touches the sides BC, CA and AB at D, E 
and F respectively.

	 It is given that BD = 8 and CD = 6 cm.
	 Since lengths of two tangents drawn from an external 

point to a circle are equal, therefore
		 BF = BD = 8 cm, CE = CD = 6 cm and let AF = AE = x cm.
	 Then, the sides of the triangle are 14 cm, (x + 6) cm 

and (x + 8) cm.
	 ∴		  2s	 = 14 + (x + 6) + (x + 8)
					    = 28 + 2x  or  s = 14 + x
				   s – a	 = 14 + x – 14 = x,

S chand Mathematics for Class X



CIRCLES    721

				   s – b	 = 14 + x – x – 6 = 8
	 and,		 s – c	 = 14 + x – x – 8 = 6
	 ∴		  Area (∆ ABC)	 = s(s – a)(s – b)(s – c)

					    = (14 + x)(x)(8)(6) = 48(x2 + 14x)
	 Also,	 Area (∆ ABC)	 = Area (∆ OBC) + Area (∆ OCA) + Area (∆ OAB)

1 1 1
					    = × BC ×OD + ×CA ×OE + × AB ×OF

2 2 2
1 1 1

					    = × 14 × 4 + × (x + 6)× 4 + × (x + 8)× 4
2 2 2

					    = 2(14 + x + 6 + x + 8) = 2(28 + 2x)

	 ∴		  48(x2 + 14x) 	 = 2(28 + 2x) = 4(14 + x)

	 Squaring, we get
				   48(x2 + 14x)	 = 16(14 + x)2

	 or		  3(x2 + 14x)	 = 196 + 28x + x2

	 or		  2x2 + 14x – 196	 = 0  or  x2 + 7x – 98 = 0
	 or		  (x – 7)(x + 14)	 = 0  i.e.,  x = 7  or  x = – 14
	 But x cannot be negative.
	 ∴		  x	 = 7
	 Hence, the sides AB and AC are 15 cm and 13 cm respectively.	
Ex. 19.	 Prove that opposite sides of a quadrilateral circumscribing a circle subtend 

supplementary angles at the centre of circle.	 [NCERT Textbook]
Sol.	 Let a circle with centre O touches the sides AB, BC, CD and DA of a quadrilateral 

ABCD at the points P, Q, R and S respectively.
	 We are to prove that
				   ∠AOB + ∠COD	 = 180°
	 and		  ∠AOD + ∠BOC	 = 180°
	 Join OP, OQ, OR and OS.
	 Since the two tangents drawn from an external point to a 

circle subtend equal angles at the centre, therefore
		 ∠1	 = ∠2, ∠3 = ∠4, ∠5 = ∠6 and ∠7 = ∠8.
	 Now, ∠1 + ∠2 + ∠3 + ∠4 + ∠5 + ∠6 + ∠7 + ∠8 = 360°	

                    [Q Sum of all the angles around a point is 360°]
	 So,	 2(∠2 + ∠3 + ∠6 + ∠7)	= 360°
	 and	 2(∠1 + ∠8 + ∠4 + ∠5)	= 360°
	 So,	 (∠2 + ∠3) + (∠6 + ∠7)	= 180°
	 and	 (∠1 + ∠8) + (∠4 + ∠5)	= 180°
	 So,	 ∠AOB + ∠COD	= 180°
		 [Q ∠2 + ∠3 = ∠AOB, ∠6 + ∠7 = ∠COD, ∠1 + ∠8 = ∠AOD and ∠4 + ∠5 = ∠BOC]
	 and	 ∠AOD + ∠BOC	= 180°	 Proved.

TOPICS
	 1.	Division of a line segment in a given ratio: (a) Internally (b) Externally	
	 2.	Tangent to a circle from a point outside it.
	 3.	Construction of triangle similar to given triangle.
	 4.	Construction of quadrilateral similar to given quadrilateral.

CONCEPT – 1 
(a)	 INTRODUCTION

We have already done certain constructions, e.g., bisecting an angle, drawing 
perpendicular bisector of a line segment, some constructions of triangles, etc., with 
rular and compass in previous class. Now, we shall do some more constructions, 
e.g., division of line segment, construction of tangent to a circle and constructions of 
similar triangles.

(b)	 DIVISION OF A LINE INTERNALLY
	 Construction 1.

Divide a line segment 4.2 cm long internally in the 
ratio of 5:3. Also, write the steps of construction.

Given. A line segment AB = 4.2 cm.
Required. To divide the line segment AB in the ratio 

5:3 internally.

Steps of construction
1. Draw AB = 4.2 cm.
2. Construct an acute angle BAX downwards.
3. On AX make 5 + 3, i.e., 8 equal parts, and mark them as A1, A2, A3, A4, A5, ... A8.
4. Join B to A8. From A5 draw A5C || A8B. C is the required point and AC : CB = 5 : 3.

Justification
Let us justify this method with the help of the following steps:
In D ABA8,
CA5 is parallel to BA8

	 Required. To divide a line segment PQ externally in the ratio 3:5.
	 Steps of construction.

    that

    externally.
	 Thus, segment PQ has been divided externally in the ratio 3 : 5 by R.

CONCEPT – 3
(a)  To draw the tangent to a circle at a given point on it, when the centre of the circle 

                 is known.
Given. A circle with centre O and a point P on it.
Required. To draw the tangent to the circle at P.
Steps of construction.

	 (i)	 Join OP.
	 (ii)	 Draw a line AB perpendicular to OP at the 

point P. APB is the required tangent at P.

Ex. 6.	 Construct a tangent to a circle of radius 4 cm from a point on the concentric circle of radius 
6 cm and measure its length. Also, verify the measurement by actual calculation.

[NCERT Textbook]
Sol.	 Steps of Construction:
	 1.	 Take a point O and draw two concentric circles of radii 

4 cm and 6 cm respectively.
	 2.	 Mark a point P on the bigger circle.
	 3.	 Join OP and bisect it. Let M be its mid-point.
	 4.	 With M as centre and MP as radius, draw a circle to 

intersect the smaller circle at Q and R.
	 5.	 Join PQ and PR. Then, PQ and PR are the required 

tangents.
	 On measurement, we find that PQ = PR = 4.5 cm (approx.).
	 Calculation: From ∆ OQP.
				              OP2 = OQ2 + PQ2   ⇒   62 = 42 + PQ2 ⇒ PQ2 = 36 – 16 = 20
	 So,                  PQ = 20  cm = 4.47 cm (approx.)
	 Similarly,       PR = 4.47 cm (approx.)
	 Justification:
	 On joining OQ, we find that ∠PQO = 90°, as ∠PQO is the angle in a semi-circle.
	 ∴	 	 PQ	 ⊥ OQ.
	 Since OQ is the radius of the given circle, so PQ has to be a tangent to the circle. 

Similarly, PR is also a tangent to the circle.		
Ex. 7.	 Draw a pair of tangents to a circle of radius 5 cm which are inclined to each other 

at an angle of 60°.			   [NCERT Textbook]
Sol.	 Steps of Construction:
	 1.	 With O as centre and radius = 5 cm, draw a circle.
	 2.	 Draw any diameter AOC.
	 3.	 Draw a radius OL such that ∠COL = 60° (i.e., the given angle).
	 4.	 At L, draw LM ⊥ OL.
	 5.	 At A, draw AN ⊥ OA.
	 6.	 These two perpendiculars intersect each other at P.
	 Then, PA and PL are the required tangents.
	 Justification:
	 Since OA is the radius, so PA has to be a tangent to the 

circle.
	 Similarly, PL is the tangent to the circle.
			  ∠APL	= 360° – ∠OAP – ∠OLP – ∠AOL
				  = 360° – 90° – 90° – (180° – 60°)

S chand Mathematics for Class X



CONSTRUCTIONS    771

				  = 360° – 360° + 60° = 60°
	 Thus, tangents PA and PL are inclined to each other at an angle of 60°.

12 Area Related to Circles

TOPICS
	 1.	Area of circle	 2. Area of sector	 3. Area of segment
	 4.	Circumference of circle	 5. Length of arc	 6. Perimeter of sector
	 7.	Area of minor segment	 8. Area of major segment
	 9.	Applications of perimeters and area of sectors, segments and circles.
INTRODUCTION

We already know how to find out perimeter and area of simple plane figures such 
as rectangle, square, parallelogram, rhombus, etc. In this chapter we shall learn to find out 
the perimeter and area of circular figures. We shall also learn to find perimeters and areas 
of sector and segment of a circle and their combinations.

CONCEPT – 1 
(a)	 CIRCLE

Circle is the locus of a point which moves in such a way that its distance 
from a fixed point O remains constant.

The fixed point O is called the centre and the constant distance is called 
its radius (r).

In our daily life, we come across too many circular shapes such as (i) bangle, (ii) coin of 
a rupee (iii) cycle wheel, (iv) moon, (v) sun, (vi) wheel of cart, (vii) sunflower, (viii) papad, etc.

SUN

Papad

788



AREA RELATED TO CIRCLES    789

(b)	 CIRCUMFERENCE
The perimeter (boundary) of a circle is called its circumference. It is the distance covered 

by travelling once around a circle.
Circumference of a circle bears a constant ratio with its diameter. The constant ratio 

is denoted by the Greek letter p (pi).

Circumference
		  	= π

Diameter
Curcumference = p.diameter = p(2r) = 2pr, where r is the radius of circle.
The great Indian Mathematician Arya Bhatta (born 476 A.D.) gave the approximate 

value of π.
62832

		  π	= 
20,000

The great mathematical genius Srinivas (1887 – 1920 A.D.) has calculated the value 
of p correct to million places of decimal with the help of this formula.

We also know that p is an irrational number non-terminating and non-recurring 
22

decimal. But for practical purposes we take p =  or p = 3.14.
7

illustrate the process of calculating areas of combination of figures in the following examples.

Ex. 3.	 Prove that area of a circular path of uniform width h surrounding a circular region 

of radius r is πh (h + 2r).

	 The radius of inner circle = r.

		  Area of the path	= Area of outer circle – Area of inner circle

			  = p(r + h)2 − pr2  = p(r2 + h2 + 2rh)− pr2

			  = p(h2 + 2rh)  = πh(h + 2r).	 Proved.

SOLUTIONS FOR NCERT TEXTBOOK EXERCISES
  NCERT EXERCISE 12.1 

   1.	 The radii of two circles are 19 cm and 9.0 cm respectively. Find the radius of the circle 
which has circumference equal to the sum of circumferences of the two circles.

Sol.	 Let radius of required circle = r cm
	 So according to condition 	2πr	=	2πr1 + 2πr2	

[where r1 = 19.0 cm & r2 = 9.0 cm]
	 ⇒		   2πr	 =	 2π × 19 + 2π × 9
	 ⇒		  r	 =	 19 + 9 = 28.0 cm
   2.	 The radii of two circles are 8 cm and 6 cm respectively. Find the radius of the circle 

N having area equal to the sum of the areas of the two circles.

C Sol.	 Let radius of required circle = r cm

    7.	 The numerical value of the area of a circle is greater than the numerical value of its 

circumference. Is this statement true ? Why ?
Sol.	 False (Not always).
    8.	 If the length of an arc of a circle of radius r is equal to that of an arc of a circle of radius 

2 r, then the angle of the corresponding sector of the first circle is double the angle of 
the corresponding sector of the other circle. Is this statement false ? Why ?

Sol.	 True, Let central angle of circle of radius r = θ1

    9.	 The area of two sectors of two different circles with equal corresponding arc lengths 

are equal. Is this statement true ? Why ?
Sol.	 False, It depend upon length of radius also not only on length of arcs.

N   10.	 The areas of two sectors of two different circles are equal. Is it necessary that their 
C corresponding arc lengths are equal ? Why ?

E Sol.	 False: It will true if arcs of same circle or of congruent circles. But not for circles of 
different radii.

M   12.	 Circumference of two circles are equal. Is it necessary that their areas be equal ? 
P Why ?

L Sol.	 True: If circumferences of two or more circles are equal then their radii are bound to 
be equal. So their areas will also be equal.

A    13.	 Areas of two circles are equal. Is it necessary that their circumferences are equal ? 
R Why ?

Sol.	 True. If areas of two or more circles are equal then their radii are also equal so their 
circumferences are bound to be equal.

13 Surface Areas &
Volumes

TOPICS
	 1.	 Surface area of solids like cuboid, cube, cylinder, cone, sphere, hemisphere and 

their combination. 
	 2.	 Volumes of shapes cube, cuboid, cylinder, cone, sphere, hemisphere and their 

combination.
	 3.	 Conversion of solid from one shape to other.
	 4.	 Surface area and volume of frustum of a cone.

INTRODUCTION
In previous class, we have learnt how to find out surface area and volume of the solids 

like cuboid, cylinder, cone, sphere, etc.
In our daily life we come across a number of solids made up of combination of two 

or more of the above solids. For example:

	 1.	 Test Tube: Its shape is combination of cylinder and hemisphere. 
It is used in chemistry laboratory.

	 2.	 Conical flask: Its shape is combination of cylinder and 
frustum of a cone. It is also used in chemistry labora-
tory.

	 3.	 Funnel: Its shape is combination of frustum of a cone and a cylinder 
and open at both the ends. It is used for transfer of liquid from one 
vessel to other.

	 4.	 Tanker: Its shape is combination of cylinder with two 
hemispherical ends. It is used to carry water, petroleum 
product, etc.

853



854    S. Chand’s MATHEMATICS FOR CLASS X

	 5.	 Tent (Circus): Its shape is cylinder mounted with a cone.

	 6.	 Capsule: Its shape is cylindrical with two hemispherical ends. It 
is used as medicine.

	 7.	 Rocket: Its shape is combination of cone and cylinder.

	 8.	 Toy (Lattu): It is a solid which is made up of 
wooden hemisphere and a cone.

Ex. 1.	 Ahmed makes cardboard boxes of two different sizes. The bigger dimensions 20 
cm, 15 cm and 5 cm and the smaller dimensions 16 cm, 12 cm and 4 cm. 5% of the 
total surface area is required extra for all overlaps. If the cost of the card board is 
` 20 for one square meter, find the cost of the cardboard for supplying 200 boxes of 
each kind.

Sol.	 Length of the bigger box	=	 20 cm
	 Breadth of the bigger box	=	15 cm
	 Height of the bigger box	=	 5 cm
		 Total surface area of box	= 2(lb + bh + hl)
			                                      = 2[20 × 15 + 15 × 5 + 5 × 20]
			                                      = 2[300 + 75 + 100]	
			                                      = 2[475] = 950 cm2

	 Area of cardboard sheet required for the construction of 200 bigger boxes
			  = 200 × 950 = 190000 cm2 = 19 m2

	 Length of the smaller box = 16 cm
	 Breadth of the smaller box = 12 cm
	 Height of the smaller box = 4 cm
		 Total surface area of smaller box	 = 2[lb + bh + hl] = 2[16 × 12 + 12 × 4 + 4 × 16]	
			  = 2[192 + 48 + 64] = 2[304] = 608 cm2

	 Area of cardboard sheet required for the construction of 200 smaller boxes
			  = 200 × 608 = 121600 cm2 = 12.16 m2

	 Area of cardboard sheet required for the construction of 200 bigger boxes and 200 
smaller boxes = (19 + 12.16) m2 = 31.16 m2

		 Extra surface for all overlaps = 5%

Ex. 2.	 The length of a cold storage is double its breadth. Its height is 3 metres. The areas 

of its four walls (including doors) is 108 m2. Find its volume.
Sol.	 Let the length, breadth and height of the cold storage be l, b and h m respectively. 

Then, l = 2b (given) and h = 3 m
	 Now,	area of the four walls	= 108 m2

	 ⇒		  2(l + b)h	 = 108   ⇒  2(2b + b) × 3 = 108	
	 ⇒		  18 b	 = 108   ⇒  b = 6 m
	 ⇒		  l	 = 2b     ⇒  l = 2 × 6 = 12 m
	 Hence, volume of the cold storage = l × b × h = 12 × 6 × 3 = 216 m3

CONCEPT 2: SURFACE AREA OF A COMBINATION OF SOLIDS
Suppose we have to find out the surface area of the conical 

tent. First we have to break it down into smaller problems that 
we have already solved. Here we see that the conical tent is made 
up of a cone and a cylinder. As we see the figure, we find part I 
i.e., cone and part II i.e., cylinder. If we put the plane surface of 
part I on the plane surface of part II and then we see the newly 
formed object. We find the surface of the newly formed object 
is the curved surface of cone and curved surface of cylinder. It 
shows that the surface area of the tent is the sum of the curved 
surface area of the cone and the curved surface area of cylinder. 

Total surface area of the tent = Curved surface area of the 
cone + Curved surface area of the cylinder.

Suppose we want to make a Lattu (toy), we take a hemisphere and a cone. We place 
the flat surface of the hemisphere on the flat surface of the cone. Here radius of the base of 
the hemisphere is equal to the radius of the top of the cone. When we have to colour the 
surface of the Lattu, the surface to be coloured consists of the curved surface of the hemi-
sphere and the curved surface of the cone.

CONCEPT – 3 : VOLUME OF A COMBINATION OF SOLIDS
In this article we shall learn how to calculate the volumes of solids 

made up of combination of two basic solids. The volume of the solid formed 
by joining two basic solids will actually be the sum of the volumes of the 
constituents. 

For example, the volume of the lattu = Volume of hemisphere + Vol-
ume of conical part.

CONCEPT – 4 : CONVERSION OF SOLID FROM ONE SHAPE TO ANOTHER 

        Anchal was playing with clay. She prepared a ball from 
that clay. Palak joined Anchal. She asked Anchal to give the 
ball. Anchal offered the ball to Palak. She felt happy to get 
the ball of clay. She immediately pressed the ball by hand to 
form a circular disc.
        If we suppose the new shape is also solid. Then clearly 
the volume of the ball and that of the circular disc will be the 
same. So, we should remember that when we come across 
objects which have got converted from one shape to another the volume remains the same.

CONCEPT – 5 : FRUSTUM OF A CONE
Frustum of a cone is the solid obtained after removing the upper portion of the cone by 

a plane parallel to its base. The lower portion, as shown in the fig., is the frustum of a cone.
Height. The perpendicular distance between the aforesaid plane and the base is called 

the height of the frustum.

(a)	 VOLUME OF A FRUSTUM OF A CONE

p

	 3.		 How many cubic centimetres of iron is required to construct an open box whose X
external dimensions are 36 cm, 25 cm and 16.5 cm provided the thickness of the iron E
is 1.5 cm. If one cubic cm of iron weighs 7.5 g, find the weight of the box. M

Sol.		 External length of open box = 36 cm
		  External breadth of open box = 25 cm P
		  External height of open box = 16.5 cm L
		  Thickness of iron = 1.5 cm A
		  So,	 Internal length	= 36 – 2 × 1.5 = 33 cm R
			   Internal breadth	= 25 – 2 × 1.5 = 22 cm
		  and	 Internal height	= 16.5 – 1.5 = 15 cm	 [ box is open]

S chand Mathematics for Class X



926    S. Chand’s MATHEMATICS FOR CLASS X

		  Hence,	 Volume of metal	= External volume – Internal volume
				   = 36 × 25 × 16.5 – 33 × 22 × 15

14 Statistics

 TOPICS
	 1.	 Introduction	 2.	 Mean of grouped data	 3.	 Mode of grouped data
	 4.	 Median of grouped data
	 5.	 Graphical representation of cumulative frequency distribution

INTRODUCTION
Statistics is defined as the science of collection, organisation, presentation, analysis and 

interpretation of numerical data. (According to Croxton and Cowden).
Raw data is a collection of actual information that is used to make logical inferences. 

The raw data is so large that it will not be easily understood. First of all data is condensed 
and presented in the form of frequency table. We generally observe a tendency in the data 
to cluster around a certain value. Then, single value represents the whole set of raw data. 
Such a representative is called a measure of central tendency or an average. The common 
average is arithmetic mean. Other measures of central tendency are median, mode, harmonic 
mean, geometric mean. Here, in this chapter, we will study arithmetic mean only.
Series

There are two types of series:
1.  Inclusive or Discrete Series
2.  Exclusive or Continuous Series.

Inclusive or Discrete Series
Let us consider the following series:
The number of patients attending a hospital in different months is given below:

Number of patients 1 – 10 11 – 20 21 – 30 31 – 40 41 – 50 51 – 60
Number of days

12 16 19 17 14 12
(in a month)

In the above table all the numbers of patients are integers and it is not possible that 
the number may be in fraction.

The patients are grouped as 1 – 10 and 11 – 20

934



STATISTICS    935

1 – 10 and 11 – 20 are discrete (discontinuous series) as there is no patient between 
10 and 11.

Definition. When the class intervals are so fixed that the upper limit of the 
class is included in the same class interval. Then such series are known as 
inclusive series.

In class 20 – 25, the upper limit 25 is included in this class itself.
Exclusive or Continuous Series

Let us consider the following series:
The distribution of heights of 40 students of a certain class in a certain city is given 

below:
Height (in cm) 150 – 155 155 – 160 160 – 165 165 – 170 170 – 175
Number of students 5 13 9 7 6

In the above table height may be in fraction of a cm. There is no gap between the upper 
limit of Ist class (150 – 155) and the lower limit of IInd class (155 – 160).
A difficulty arises if there is a gap between the upper limit (155 cm) of Ist class and 
lower limit (155 cm) of the IInd class. Because the height (155.4 cm or 155.5 cm) in the 
gap between 155 cm and 156 are possible.
This is exclusive or continuous series.

Definition: In the exclusive or continuous series, the upper limit of one class is 
the lower limit of next class. The common point (155 cm) of two classes is included 
in higher class (155 – 160) and not in the lower class (150 – 155).

Working rule to convert a discontinuous series into continuous series 
(Inclusive series to exclusive series)

Step 1. Find the adjustment factor by the following formula
1

      Adjustment factor =  [Lower limit of second class – Upper limit of first class]
2

Step 2. 	Subtract the adjustment factor from the lower limit and add to the upper limit 
of each class. We will get exclusive series.

For example : We consider the following inclusive series 11 – 20, 21 – 30, 31 – 40.
1 1

Step 1. 	Adjustment factor =  [21 – 20] =  = 0.5
2 2

Step 2. 	The inclusive series is converted into 
	 exclusive series:
	 11 – 0.5 —— 20 + 0.5     i.e.; 10.5 —— 20.5, Inclusive form Exclusive form

	 21 – 0.5 —— 30 + 0.5     i.e.; 20.5 —— 30.5, 11 – 20 10.5 – 20.5
	 31 – 0.5 —— 40 + 0.5     i.e.; 30.5 —— 40.5 21 – 30 20.5 – 30.5

31 – 40 30.5 – 40.5

CONCEPT – 1 : ARITHMETIC MEAN
TYPE – 1: A.M. of Ungrouped Data

Arithmetic mean of raw data (when frequencies are not given)
The arithmetic mean of a raw data is obtained by adding all the values of the variables 

and dividing the sum by total number of values that are added.
Let the values of the variables x are x1, x2, ..., xn, where n is the total number of values, 

then

The arithmetic mean of a set of observations is equal to their sum divided by the total 
number of observations.

TYPE – 3: Grouped frequency distribution
         Sometimes the data is so large that it is inconvenient to list every item in the frequency 
distribution table. Then we group the items into convenient intervals and the data is 
presented in a frequency-distribution in which each class interval contains five or ten values 
of the variate generally. The mid-value of each class is the representative of each item falling 
in that interval.

Here individual values lose their identity. If we assume that all values falling in a 
class interval are equal to the middle value of this class interval. This middle value is called 
mid-value, mid-point or class mark.

In order to make life easy and save time and energy following methods are adopted 
for calculation purposes:
	 (I)	 Direct method
	 (II)	 Assumed mean deviation method
	 (III)	 Step deviation method

(a)	 Direct method for calculation of mean

(b)	 Assumed mean method

If the values of x are large, then the calculation of the arithmetic mean by direct method 
becomes lengthy and tedius. To avoid such lengthy calculations, we use short cut method. 
In this method, the labour of calculation becomes less.

In this method, we choose assumed mean ‘a’ (say) and subtract it from each of the 
values xi. The reduced value  xi – a is called the deviation of xi from a. The deviations are

CONCEPT – 2 : WEIGHTED MEAN
We have calculated the mean by assuming that all items in the distribution have equally 

important, but the importance of different items may not be the same.
For example in tenth class Computer and Hindi are not equally important. Clearly, 

Computer is more important than any other subject. In fact, weightage of Computer in 
comparison to Hindi is much more. In such a case we assign weights to different items. The 
term weight stands for relative importance of different items. The rate assigned to an item 
is proportional to the importance of the item.

S chand Mathematics for Class X



948    S. Chand’s MATHEMATICS FOR CLASS X

Definition. If x1, x2, ..., xn denote n values of a variable x and w1, w2, 
..., wn denote respectively their weights, then their weighted mean, xw  is 
given by

n

∑wi xi

                                            x  = i=1
w n

∑wi
i=1

The weights represent the relative importance of the values of the variable x. For 
example, prices are usually weighted by the relative quantities involved.

(c)	 Properties of Arithmetic Mean
n

	 I.	 If x1, x2, x3, .., xn are n observations with mean x , then ∑(xi − x)  = 0.	  
		  i.e., the algebraic sum of deviations from mean is zero. i=1

	II. 	If the mean of n observations x1, x2, x3, ..., xn is x , then the mean of the observations x1 + 
a, x2 + a, x3 + a, ..., xn + a is x  + a. 

		  i.e., if each observation is increased by a, then the mean is also increased by a. 

	III.	If x  is the mean of n observations x1, x2, ..., xn; then the mean of x1 – a, x2 – a, ... xn– a is 
x – a,  where a is any real number.

		  i.e., If each observation is decreased by a, then the mean is also decreased by a.	
	IV.	 The mean of n observations x1, x2, x3, ..., xn is x . If each observation is multiplied by a, then 

the mean of the new observations is a x , where a is any number other than zero.
	V.	 If the mean of n observations x1, x2, x3, ...., xn is x , the mean of the observations of 

x1 x
, 2 x3 x x

, , ..., n  is , where a is any non-zero number.
a a a a a

		  i.e., if each observation is divided by a non-zero number, then the mean is also divided by it.

CONCEPT – 4 : MODE

Mode is the size of the variable which occurs most frequently.
In discrete or ungrouped case, the mode is the variate having maximum frequency.
For example :
In the series 6, 5, 3, 4, 3, 7, 8, 5, 9, 5, 4 we notice that 5 occurs most frequently therefore 

5 is the mode.
Mode is also known as norm. 

Ex. 1.	 A shoe shop in Janakpuri had sold hundred pairs of shoes of a particular brand 
in a certain day with the following distribution.

Size of the shoes 4 5 6 7 8 9 10
No. of pairs sold 10 15 20 35 16 3 1

	 Find mode of the distribution.
Sol.	 We have,

Size of the shoes 4 5 6 7 8 9 10
No. of pairs sold 10 15 20 35 16 3 1

	 In the above table we notice that the size 7 has the maximum frequency, i.e., 35.
	 Therefore 7 is the mode of the distribution.
Types of Modal Series
	 (i)	 Unimodal series. The series which contains one mode.
	 (ii)	 Bimodal series. The series which contains two modes.
	 (iii)	 Trimodal series. The series which contains three modes.

ILL-DEFINED MODE. If a series has more than one mode then the mode is said to 
be ill-defined.

Mode of a grouped distribution

we can find the “modal class” which is the class having maximum frequency.

	 (i)	 Mode is readily comprehensively and easy to calculate. It can be located in some

	 (ii)	 Mode is not at all affected by extreme values.
	 (iii)	 Mode can be conveniently found even for class interval of unequal magnitude.

(c)	 Demerits of mode
	 (i)	 Mode is ill-defined. In some cases we may come across two modes.
	 (ii)	 It is not based upon all the observations.
	 (iii)	 No further mathematical treatment is possible in case of mode.
	 (iv)	 Mode is affected to a greater extent by fluctuations of sampling.

(d)	 Uses of mode 
Mode is used to find the ideal size e.g., Readymade garments, shoes etc.

(a)	 Merits of median
	 (i)	 It is rigidly defined.
	 (ii)	 It is easily understood and easy to calculate.
	 (iii)	 It is not at all affected by extreme values.
	 (iv)	 It can be located graphically.
	 (v)	 It can be determined even by inspection in some cases.
	 (vi)	 It can be located if the class interval be unequal.

(b)	 Demerits of median
	 (i)	 In case of even number of observations median cannot be determined exactly.
	 (ii)	 It is not based on all the observations.
	 (iii)	 It is not subject to algebraic treatment.
	 (iv)	 It is much affected by fluctuations of sampling.

(c)	 Uses of median
	 (i)	 Median is the only average to be used while dealing with qualitative data 

which cannot be measured quantitatively but can be arranged in ascending or 
desending order of magnitude.

	 (ii)	 It is used for determining the typical value in problems concerning wages; 
distribution of wealth etc.

(d)	 Median of grouped frequency distribution

Special Points
1. Arithmetic mean is based on all the observations. It is not useful if there are some 

extreme values in the data.
In a colony inhabited by middle class persons, chances are there that a very rich person, 

(owner of a mill) or a very poor person like a labourer with meager income may be living. 
If the income of any one of them is included for the purpose of finding the arithmetic mean, 
the result may be misleading.

2. Mode is more useful to business persons. The businessman is interested to know 
the size of pair of shoes which is sold maximum.

3. Median is useful when there are open end extreme classes, because median is not 
affected by extreme open values.

If in a class of students with normal intelligence, a brilliant student securing very 
high marks or a student securing very poor marks say 5 – 10% is admitted then arithmetic 
mean of marks obtained by the class will be misleading due to the extreme cases. In such 
cases median will be true representative because median is not affected by extreme values.

CONCEPT – 6 : CUMULATIVE FREQUENCY CURVE OR THE OGIVE
First we prepare the cumulative frequency table, then the cumulative frequencies are 

plotted against the upper or lower limits of the corresponding class intervals. By joining the 
points the curve so obtained is called a cumulative frequency curve or ogive.

There are two types of ogives:
1. Less than ogive: Plot the points with the upper limits of the class as abscissae and the 

corresponding less than cumulative frequencies as ordinates. The points are joined by free 
hand smooth curve to give less than cumulative frequency curve or the less than Ogive. It 
is a rising curve.

2. Greater than ogive: Plot the points with the lower limits of the classes as abscissa and 
the corresponding greater than cumulative frequencies as ordinates. Join the points by a 
free hand smooth curve to get the “Greater than Ogive”. It is a falling curve.

When the points obtained are joined by straight lines, the picture obtained is called 
cumulative frequency polygon.

N
Median can be obtained from cumulative frequency curve. From  frequency draw 

2

a line parallel to x-axis cutting the curve at a point. From this point draw a perpendicular 
to the axis. The point at which the perpendicular meets the x-axis determines the median.

Less than type and greater than type curves intersect at a point. From this point of 
intersection if we draw a perpendicular on the x-axis then this cuts x-axis at some point. 
This point gives the median.

SOLVED EXAMPLES

Ex. 1.	 The following distribution gives the daily income of 50 workers of a factory.

Daily income (in `) 100-120 120-140 140-160 160-180 180-200
Number of workers 12 14 8 6 10

		 Convert the distribution above to a less than type cumulative frequency distribution, 
and draw its ogive.

Sol.	 	Less than type cumulative frequency distribution:

  NCERT EXEMPLAR EXERCISE 14.2   
	 1.	 The median of an ungrouped data and the median calculated when the same data 

is grouped are always the same. Do you think that this is a correct statement ? Give 
reason.

Sol.		 Not always, because for calculating median of a grouped data, the formula used is 
based on the assumption that the observations in the classes are uniformly  distributed 
(or equal spaced).

	 2.	 In calculating the mean of grouped data, grouped in classes of equal width, we may 
use the formula,

Σf d
			                                                       x = a + i i

Σfi

		  Where, a is the assumed mean, a must be one of the mid-point of the classes. Is the last 
statement correct ? Justify your answer.

Sol.		 Not necessary, the mean of the data does not depend on the choice of a (assumed 
mean).

	 3.	 Is it true to say that the mean, mode and median of grouped data will always be 
different? Justify your answer.

Sol.		 No, it is not always the case. The values of these three measures can be the same. It 
depends on the type of data.

	 4.	 Will the median class and modal class of grouped data always be different? Justify 
your answer.

Sol.		 Not always it depend on data.
