15 Probability

TOPICS
1.	 Experiment and theoretical approach to probability.
2.	 Events, outcomes, favourable outcomes, sample space and methods of finding 

probability.
3.	 Sure events, impossible events and application of probability
4.	 Use of sample space, etc.

INTRODUCTION
In our day to day life when we are not sure of happening an event then we use the 

word ‘probably’, e.g.,
	 (i)	 Probably it may rain today.
	 (ii)	 It is possible that he may win in the election.
	 (iii)	 Probably India may win the cricket match against New-Zealand this time.
	 (iv)	 Chances of his passing in the examination are very few.

In all the above statements probably, chance, possible, etc., convey the sense of 
uncertainty about the occurrence of some particular event. It appears that there cannot be 
any exact measurement for these uncertainties, but in Mathematical Statistics we do have 
methods for calculating the degree of certainty of events in numerical value, under certain 
conditions. A measure of uncertainty is provided by a branch of Mathematics, called “Theory 
of Probability”.

When we perform experiments in science repeatedly under identical conditions, 
we get almost the same result. But, there are experiments in which the outcome may be 
different even if the experiment is performed under identical conditions. In tossing a coin 
head may come up or tail may come up we are not sure at all about the outcome. This is a 
random experiment.

The chance of happening an event when expressed quantitatively is called probability. 
However, we may give two definitions of probability.

(i)	 Experimental	 (ii)  Theoretical

1017



1018    S. Chand’s MATHEMATICS FOR CLASS X

CONCEPT–1

(a)	 Experimental Probability
Let us perform the following experiments of tossing a coin and record the number 

of heads turning up and then we calculate the respective probabilities as shown in the 
following table:

Number of trials Number of heads turning up Experimental probability
100 66 0.66
200 134 0.67
300 144 0.48
400 248 0.62
500 315 0.63
600 366 0.61
700 413 0.59
800 392 0.49
900 459 0.51
1000 500 0.50

As we increase the number of trials the 
fluctuations in the experimental probability 
gradually decreases and would be approaching 
to a fixed number in this case 0.5.

In ten million trials the experimental 
probability of heads in such cases must be 
very-very close to 0.5.

This leads to mathematical model for 
experimental probability called theoretical 
probability. The basic difference between 
these two probability is that experimental 
probability is based on what has happened 
while theoretical probability attempts to 
predict what will happen.

(b)	 Probability – Theoretical approach
If a coin is fair (unbiased) both outcomes head or tail are equally likely to come up.

2

say that outcomes of a fair die showing 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 are equally likely. The probability of 

1
showing up 1 or 2 or 3 or 4 or 5 or 6 is one out of six or .

(c)	 Some Basic Terms

A die is a well-balanced cube with its six faces marked with numbers 
(dots) from 1 to 6, one number on one face. The plural of die is dice. When 
we play a game with a die, we are generally interested in the number coming 
up after the toss on its uppermost face. The number on each of the faces is 
therefore, a possible outcome. The possibility of getting 5 on the uppermost 
face is same as that of getting any other number like 1, 2, 3, 4 or 6. Since, 
there are six equally likely outcomes, i.e., 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6 in a single throw 
of a die and there is only one way of getting 5. The possibility of the number 

1
5 coming up is 1 in 6. Hence, the probability of getting 5 is .

6

Cards: A pack of cards consists of four suits, i.e., spades 

( ), Hearts (ª), Diamonds (©) and Clubs (¨). Each suit consists 
of 13 cards, nine cards numbered 2, 3, 4, ..... 10, an Ace, a King, 
a Queen and a Jack or Knave. Colour of Spades and Clubs is 
black and that of Hearts and Diamonds is red.

Hearts, Diamonds, clubs and spades are four colours or suits of a pack. King card, 
Queen card and Jack card are called face cards. Thus there are 3 face cards in a suit and total 
of 12 face cards in a normal pack of 4 suits.

Suppose we draw a card from a deck of playing cards, then drawing of each card is a 
possible outcome. The possibility of drawing a queen of heart is the same as that of drawing 
any other card. Since, there are 52 cards in the deck, therefore there are 52 equally likely 
outcomes. But, the outcome of getting queen of heart is only one. Hence, the probability of 

1 1
drawing a queen of heart is .  Symbolically. P(queen of heart) = 

52 52
Equally likely events. Two events are said to be ‘equally likely’, if one of them cannot 

be expected in preference to the other. For instance, if we draw a card from well-shuffled 
pack, we may get any card, then the 52 different cases are equally likely.

Impossible event. In single throwing of a die, there are only six possible outcomes i.e. 
1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6. But, we are interested that a die may come up with a number 7. Since, no 
face of the die is marked with 7, so 7 cannot come under any circumstances. Hence, getting 
a number 7 is impossible. This type of event is called an impossible event.

0
		  P(getting 7)	= = 0

6
Hence, the probability of an impossible event is always zero.
Again let us understand this concept by taking another example. If we have 5 red balls 

in a bag, then the probability of drawing a green ball from that bag is always zero, since the 
bag does not contain any green ball. Thus, this is also an impossible event.

0
		  P (getting green ball)	= = 0

5
Sure event. We want to find the probability of getting a natural number less than 7 on 

throwing a die. Since, every face of a die is marked with a natural number less than 7, we 
are sure that we shall always get a natural number less than 7 whenever we throw a die.

Therefore, this event is a sure event.
6

		  P(getting a natural number)	= = 1
6

Hence, the probability of a sure event is always 1.
So, the probability of any event lies between 0 and 1.
Mathematically, 	 0 ≤ P(A) ≤ 1.

flavoured. Hence getting an orange flavoured candy is an impossible event. So 
its probability is zero.

	 (ii)	 As there are all candies of lemon flavour. So it is sure event, hence its probability 
is 1.
